inline.s: This matter of causal conditions — the transformation of what is most difficult into what is most easy — comes about because through measureless kalpas, life after life, we have flowed along in mixed defilement, and our habit of it is deep and thick. Even when a single thought of faith arises today and we begin to cut it off before evening falls, if we would stem the long current of endless kalpas, the task is truly far from easy. Even this single thought of turning the head back is exceedingly hard to bring forth. It is the wondrous sprout of good roots accumulated over kalpas; meeting its season, it first pushes out its shoot — yet its flowering and fruiting depend entirely on constant tending and protection. Otherwise it withers in an instant. Meeting circumstances and conditions, handling affairs with the Dharma, in time it becomes thoroughly familiar; add to that the work of calm and insight, and you may gradually arrive at liberation. Yet we are liberated from the very beginning. So the reason affliction is not liberated is no fault of the Dharma: it is that the mind binds and clings to itself, and so is not liberated. This is because our worldly feelings have long been thick and our habitual defilement thoroughly familiar; what is familiar is hard to forget, and so it flares up at the slightest touch. Hence the saying: I have never seen one who loves virtue as he loves beauty. If you exchange the one for the other, then what was unfamiliar becomes familiar of itself, and what was familiar becomes unfamiliar. Unfamiliar, it thins; thinning, it recedes; receding, it grows faint; faint, it is forgotten; forgotten, there is no leisure left to seek release — and of itself it no longer binds. In time the mind settles into peace, and the thousand forms and myriad shapes before you are seen as flowers in the sky and the moon in water, as heat-haze and frozen river. There was never anything to bind or cling to — so what release is there to seek? You say Sengzhao’s words on the immutability of things have served you well. Were you not a vessel of great capacity, you could not enter that old master’s gate. Yet the single line, “The sun and moon shine across the sky,” remains unclear to you. If this is unclear, then you do not understand Sengzhao; and if you do not understand him, then his words have not truly served you. This line the old man doubted for several years, until at last, within his own mind, he came to see it for himself, alone and clear. From that time on, wherever I have met conditions and found strength, it has mostly been through this old master’s words. That you believe at once upon going out the door is truly no small connection. The old man does not hesitate to speak it out plainly for you — only I fear that one day you will curse the old monk. Just take this line and lay it across your mind. In every movement, every action and undertaking; in every place of sound and form, wealth and profit; in every condition of adversity and favor; in every stirring of joy, anger, sorrow, and delight; in every choosing and rejecting, loving and hating — wherever there is any flowing, moving state, seal it at once with this seal. Apply the one seal and it is settled. Watch how it is that there is nowhere immutable; how it is that there is a place of constant stillness; how it is that there is a place that does not flow; how it is that there is a place that does not move; how it is that there is a place that does not reach around. Look and look in this way, and suddenly, with a crash, you will see through this line. Then you will know that the old man has not deceived you, and only then will you believe that the original truth does not deceive itself.
Instructions to Huang Weiheng

Though you say you aspire to the Way, the eye within you has not yet become clear. You constantly take worldly Dharma and Buddha-Dharma, the Chan school and the teaching school, and inevitably speak of them as two separate halves. If here you speak of them as two halves, then all your hating and loving, adversity and favor, choosing and rejecting, liking and disliking, success and failure, movement and stillness — fittingly, every one of them will be split into two halves as well. Haiyin has told you again and again: the buddhas and patriarchs from the first have no substantial Dharma to give to people; they only point out and expose, for each person, the matter that is originally present in his own portion. The Zongjing says: take the one mind as the source, and illumine the ten thousand dharmas as a mirror. It is precisely because we cannot know the one mind that the Buddha spoke teachings to point it out; and because we cannot see our own mind that the patriarchs borrowed Chan to show it. Both were acts of last resort. Now you say that studying the teachings leaves you mentally weary, while following Chan is like riding a favorable wind. This is only the depth of your prajñā-habit from many lives. Yet in this whole matter, from Haiyin’s side, both are empty deceptions: there is simply no talk of difficult and easy. If you do not penetrate your own mind, then Chan becomes deviant understanding and deviant defilement, and both fall into the pit of consciousness and feeling; while the teachings become deluded knowing and deluded seeing, and all come down to a handle for words and talk. Neither is the ultimate true ground. You do not realize that the teachings are the Buddha’s eye and Chan is the Buddha’s mind; the two are not two different things — how could there be this and that? When Haiyin teaches people to read the teachings and investigate Chan, it is never with views of that kind. To form such an interpretation today is not only to betray Haiyin, but to betray your own inherent spirit as well. I recall an ancient asking: the ancients ate when hungry and slept when tired, and that was the Way; people today eat when hungry and sleep when tired — why is that not the Way? The answer: the ancients, eating, simply ate; sleeping, simply slept — and so it was the Way. People today, eating, do not eat; sleeping, do not sleep; they think wildly and reckon at random — and so they turn their backs on the Way. From this we see that in your daily life you need only raise your eyebrows, give a shout — let gods be startled and ghosts afraid, let the heavenly māras’ courage shatter and the shades of the dead dissolve — one shout and they are driven back, leaving you on your original ground, silent and still, not a thread hanging, stark and bare, utterly naked. Take this one style of household. When you want to read, then read; when you do not, set it aside — do not allow a single word to hang there. When you want to write, then write; when you do not, set it aside — do not allow wild thinking and reckoning. Even in drinking tea and eating rice, simply drink tea and eat rice. When you want to sleep, then sleep; when you must relieve yourself, then relieve yourself. Meeting it, it is finished — and afterwards you must not allow a single thought of recollection, like a wandering ghost. Clean and pure, spotless and white — and yet you must not sit down inside that cleanness and purity either. Thus, single-bladed, you go straight in, one thought pressing forward: then in reading you meet the ancients face to face, and in writing you simply spit it out in one breath from your own breast, with no before and no after. The time of storing is the time of pouring forth; the time of pouring forth is the time of storing. In this way you are not turned about by movement and stillness, by light and dark, nor shifted by any of the myriad tricks. This is what is called a towering great man, a fellow beyond measure. Do you believe this? If you truly believe it, then hike up your robes and enter here. Take care, take care.
Instructions to Layman Ma

One who studies the Way must, first, be urgent in the matter of birth and death. Second, he must know that the body is the root of suffering and that the mind is the root of deluded thought and karmic creation. Third, he must truly and genuinely see through it: the fame, rank, wealth, and honor of the world, its sounds and forms, goods and profits, are all vain blossoms, unreal. Fourth, he must fear that in this life he may create evil karma and hereafter fall into hell, undergo every kind of suffering, with no one to rescue or protect him. Fifth, he must know that the root of life now present is no more than the space of a single breath: if this breath is cut off, then to seek again today’s business of investigating Chan, studying the Way, and making merit will be forever impossible — how much less the enjoyment of wealth and honor? When one who studies the Way has these five minds, and hour after hour, moment after moment, stores and piles them in his breast, then all the vain and flowery states before him grow naturally cold and faint, and the ground of his mind becomes naturally pure. What he has learned in the past, his views and knowledge, his learning, his clever talk and tricks — he sets it all down. He brings forth the bodhi-mind, forever cuts off wine and meat, coveting nothing and loving nothing, keeps the precepts and cultivates merit, performs every kind of good work, and takes these as the foundation that carries the Way. He further reads the Mahāyāna scriptures to help bring forth his own mind and open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; only then may he undertake contemplation. He contemplates only this mind: vast, perfect, and bright, pure, empty, and still, not a single dharma to be obtained. Deluded thoughts were never there, and neither is there birth or death. As for this body of faculties, all its movements are like those of a phantom man who never had a mind or consciousness; all the states before him are like flowers in the sky, suddenly arising and suddenly ceasing, originally not existing. There is only the one bright thought, perfectly clear, never obscured — and even this thought is not there. This is called right mindfulness. With the mind used in this way, throughout the six periods of the day, in movement and stillness, at leisure and in business, he is thus, unmoved. In adversity and favor, in like and dislike, foe and kin are equal. Following worldly conditions, whatever merit he performs, each act and each dharma becomes perfect and wondrous pure practice. One who practices thus is named a bodhisattva in action. If a man of the Way can truly use his mind in this way, he may be said to engage in the Buddha’s work without leaving the dust of affliction, to manifest the body of a magistrate and yet speak the Dharma; and this is what is meant by repaying the Buddha’s grace and repaying the grace of the state. Your nature is spiritually clear, and you have resolved your mind toward the Way; therefore I have specially given you these instructions, and I bestow on you the name Pure and Wondrous Layman. Do not be false to your own inherent spirit; do not forget these words. Take care.
Instructions to Wang Sheng on Seeking the Precepts and a New Style-Name

The young man Wang is named Tingzuo, styled Zizhan. He feels his given name is commonplace and his style-name trespasses upon the ancients, and asks the Phantom Man to renew them. The Phantom Man, delighted, told him: How extraordinary, your substance! The tradition has it: if you can renew yourself daily, renew day by day, and renew again each day. Now your vow is to expel the old self and make it wholly new. Not only would you renew your name; you would renew your mind. The name is the guest of reality; the mind is the reality of virtue. If you do not devote yourself to the real but prize an empty name, that is not virtue. From this we see that you are not only commonplace in name but commonplace in mind. What is meant by commonplace is not a matter of clothing, cap, speech, or appearance; it means what has been tainted and stained by long familiarity in one’s inherent virtue. Our inherent virtue is originally bright, but as day by day we steep ourselves in cravings, the eye is obscured by deviant forms, the ear by licentious sounds, the nose by foul and fragrant scents, the tongue by rich flavors, the body by false contacts, the mind by deviant thoughts. These six obscure one another and churn and darken what is within; smoked and steeped, dyed and habituated, habit becomes nature, and we call it what we originally have, call it what is naturally so. Thus we gallop far into the realm of confusion, and the virtue of original brightness is turned around and seen as something alien — how should we know there is an old self, an old self? This is what the sages grieved over; their grief lay precisely here. Therefore they cast one into the water of the precepts to wash it away. And the precepts are nothing else: they are the light of wisdom inherent in one’s own mind, which the Confucians call the bright virtue. Now, a person’s wisdom-light is not bright, and so the bright virtue darkens day by day. To restore the bright virtue and return to innate truth, one must brighten the wisdom-light and shatter the darkness and obscuration. When darkness and obscuration are broken, the original substance appears; when the wisdom-light is bright, all hindrances dissolve. This is why our Buddha established the precept against killing to perfect humaneness; the precept against stealing to fulfill righteousness; the precept against sexual misconduct to establish propriety; the precept against false speech to deepen trustworthiness; and the precept against drinking wine to brighten wisdom. When the five precepts are complete, the five constants are fulfilled; when the six senses are restrained, the three karmas are purified. This is what is called washing away old defilement, advancing in daily renewal, forsaking the old self, and creating a new transformation. Therefore the Phantom Man also changes your given name to Yan, and your style-name to Zilun, so that you may receive the Buddha’s precepts as you would a ruler’s command. Strive at it.
Instructions to Zhou Ziqian

The five colors make the eyes blind; the five notes make the ears deaf; the five flavors spoil the taste; galloping and hunting make the mind run wild. These are Laozi’s warnings. Look not at what is contrary to propriety; listen not to what is contrary to propriety; speak not what is contrary to propriety; move not in any way contrary to propriety. And again: in youth, when the blood and vital breath are not yet settled, the warning lies in matters of desire; when grown, when the blood and breath are at their fullest, the warning lies in strife; when old, when the blood and breath have declined, the warning lies in acquisitiveness. These are Confucius’s warnings. Not to kill, not to steal, not to commit sexual misconduct, not to speak falsely or with ornate words, not to speak with a double tongue or harshly, not to be greedy, hateful, or deluded. These are the Buddha’s warnings. Ah — our own nature is originally spiritually clear and pure, but because of the stains of habitual defilement it grows daily more turbid and darkened, and we sink into confusion without waking. This happens only in the space between ear, eye, mouth, nose, body, and mind as they face sounds, forms, scents, tastes, tangibles, and dharmas: stuck fast and entangled, contriving and struggling in the mind, long deluded and never turning back. Therefore the sages, in pity, earnestly made these warnings for us; and further, they wished to expel old defilement, cut off the habits of the dust, and restore our originally pure true mind. From this we see that the precepts are in me and are complete in the mind; cultivate them with the body — this is what is meant by the Way not being far from man. Hence it is said: Is the sage far off? Embody him and he is spirit. If we would reach the source of the great Way, it lies only in reverently upholding this. Master Zhou is young and has set his will earnestly on the highest; he has turned his mind to this, and so I have written these words to show him.
Instructions to the Novice Zuding

You have seen the markets and shops of the world: butchers’ stalls laid out in rows, and every passerby, without exception, eyeing them and watering at the mouth, hoping for a taste of one slice. Such is ordinary feeling. Yet whenever I see our own kind — those who call themselves śramaṇas, sons of Śākyamuni — dwelling amid a grove of sandalwood, treading ground of coolness, passing through the marketplace of the great Dharma where the supreme sweet dew and the wondrous flavor of ambrosia lie spread out, they look askance at it as though it were poison. Is this not pitiable? Still, this is the fault of not knowing the flavor. If they knew it, how would they yield to the passion for a slice of meat? Our Buddha, at his first appearance in the world, at once held up the Prātimokṣa before people. This was to spread the sweet dew along the highway, hoping that everyone might taste it and enter together the land of no death. And how many, passing by, have tasted it? I came by chance to Rājagṛha and stopped in the Maitreya Grove, where it happened that a stall of sweet dew was opened. A novice named Zuding came from Wuxing to call on me and asked about the adornment of Buddha-lands and the supreme Dharma-door. So I pointed him into the grove, and there he partook of and discerned the flavor of this sweet-dew Dharma. What is called the sweet-dew Dharma is precisely the four fundamental grave precepts. Alas, people have long been steeped in the arena of birth and death, perfecting the iron bed and its instruments of torment — and none of it is established apart from these four: lust, killing, theft, and falsehood. As for the adornments of all the buddhas’ Pure Lands, they too are accomplished only by cutting off these four. Hence the saying: only when the lustful mind is forever cut off can the Buddha-way be accomplished. Now the novice wishes to clear away rubble and make a monastery, to turn a defiled land into a Pure Land. Unless he overturns the four roots and makes of them four pools of coolness, how can he transform the three poisons into three kinds of ground of liberation? Therefore the old man Haiyin praised him, saying: Son of the Buddha, if you wish to accomplish the Dharma-door of inexhaustible merit, you should learn well this Prātimokṣa and take it as the supreme truth. All Dharma-doors enter from here.
Instructions to Wu Gongmin

Subhūti asked the Buddha: how should one dwell? How should one subdue one’s mind? The Buddha answered: thus should one dwell; thus should one subdue one’s mind. And again he said: one should give rise to the mind that dwells nowhere. And again: when faith is pure, the true mark is immediately produced. Yet the true mark has no mark — how can there be production? Indeed, because production is itself non-production, dwelling is fundamentally non-dwelling. When faith is like this, the five aggregates are cool, and in a single thought all is suddenly empty and every delusion is perfectly extinguished. Such subduing is no subduing; it is called subduing. Gongmin’s faith is very deep. He asked me to confer on him the bodhisattva precepts, and further asked for a method of holding the mind. I told him the method of taming and subduing in just this way, and further changed his style-name to Taming and Subduing. As for marks being precisely no-marks, one must not take no-marks as no-marks; therefore I also had him engrave a fixed daily lesson, so that through daily practice without shifting, in time it becomes wholly one, all marks are extinguished, and he suddenly concurs with the unborn. This is what is meant by: when faith is pure, the true mark is immediately produced.
Instructions to the Two Masters Cheng and Hong

The saying goes: if a gentleman has no gravity, he has no dignity, and his learning will not be solid. And again: with nothing to command within, he cannot stand; with nothing upright without, he cannot walk. These words are small, but they may illustrate great matters. Thus, in worldly and world-transcending learning of the way of sages and worthies, there has never been one who reached the extension of knowledge, the investigation of things, and the clarity of mind and seeing of nature without beginning from rectifying the mind, making the will sincere, and cultivating the person. Therefore Confucius, in practicing humaneness, put the three daily self-examinations and the four prohibitions first; and our Buddha, in governing the mind, took the three karmas and the seven branches of the body and speech as the root. Surveying figures ancient and modern, high and low, those who became great vessels, carried out great enterprises, illumined the cosmos, and stood out as models for others — none of them reached that from this, reached the utmost refinement from the coarse, reached the far from the near, by any other way. Scholars today mostly take mouth and ear learning for true learning, their own views for genuine investigation, idle talk for accommodating others, self-indulgence for following their feelings, slouching compliance for tolerance of the crowd, unbridled license for nourishing the will, comfort and full belly for regulating the body, discursive thinking for rectifying the mind, tight restraint for tormenting the body, dignified bearing for arrogance, restraining thoughts for self-torture, strict observance for pretension, the Way and its work for superfluous goods, this body and world for diamond indestructibility, and birth and death for a side matter. The person is not established, the mind is not investigated, the work of the Way is not accomplished, learning is not refined: this is why the world grows daily lower and the Way daily weaker, the mind daily duller and the will daily more lost, manners daily more slack and conduct daily thinner, the teaching daily more decayed and the Dharma daily more ruined. Chasing wind and catching shadows, later students have nothing to rely on. If we hope to see in those who cultivate a quality of wholeness and purity, how could that be possible? Confucius said: a sage I cannot get to see; could I but see a man of constancy, that would do. Hence the Duke of Zhou’s dream and the sigh over the phoenix bird. How could a gentleman who has set his will allow himself to be easy with himself? Strive, both of you.
Instructions to Jiang Wuyu

For ten years I have spoken bitter words to you, like teaching a drunkard to fast and be solemn. Not that he is not gravely reverent — but his very reverence is still the manner of a drunkard. Now, reading your letter in your own hand, I suddenly feel as though I have woken from a drunken dream. It makes my heart ache and then leap with joy. Since all the world is drunk, if everyone were like you, then I should not prize being the only sober one. I have often said: Su Qin was a man of mere tongue and mouth; the wealth and honor he set his heart on gave him no proper direction, yet whenever he indulged himself in slackness, he tied himself to a beam and pricked his thigh with an awl, and in the end he got what he wanted. How much more does a world-transcending sage or worthy outweigh one such man, and the supreme wondrous Way outweigh much gold! The King of Yue suffered the shame of Kuaiji and vowed to avenge himself on Wu, so he slept on brushwood and tasted gall for more than twenty years, and in the end became hegemon. Yet the craving of kalpas outweighs the feud with Wu; imprisonment in birth and death and the torment and disgrace of this body outweigh the shame of Kuaiji. If you do not cherish a hatred that grinds the teeth, if you forget the resolve to sleep on brushwood and taste gall, if you cannot spur yourself on by tying yourself to a beam and pricking your thigh — how will you repay your first resolve and wipe away the great shame? I have heard it said: the highest is to establish virtue; next, to establish merit; next, to establish a name. If you can truly spur yourself on by the highest, then poverty itself is a joy, and what business have other things to entangle your mind? Confucius said: a scholar who sets his will on the Way but is ashamed of poor clothes and poor food is not worth conversing with. The ancients also said: if one has the joy of the Way and righteousness, the body itself may be set outside. If the body may be set outside, then beyond this there is nothing to do — how could anything entangle the mind? How could one occupy such a place and not be at peace? May you strive at it.
Instructions to Wang Muchang and Zhou Shifu

I have often said: of all things born in the world, man alone is most spiritually aware — this is an old saying. I, however, say it is not so. Why? Man and all things alike possess the nature of spiritual awareness; this nature is equally bestowed and commonly endowed. Where was there ever a gap between man and things? In the end, what makes man different from things is only that things possess it without knowing, while man knows what he possesses. To know one’s original endowment and exhaust it is called a sage; to know it should be exhausted but be unable to exhaust it at once is called a worthy; to know and be willing to seek its exhaustion is called wise; to know and be unwilling to turn back and seek it is called foolish; to know without being true, and to seek beyond measure, is called mad; to know without clarity, and to hold one small corner as necessarily right, is called rigid; and as for not knowing and yet seeking wildly, that is called bizarre. Not to know and not to seek leaves one merely a thing. Alas — this difference between man and thing lies only between knowing and not knowing, seeking and not seeking. Though the distance is the width of a hair, the loss is a thousand li. Surveying the gentlemen of the three Qi regions, who does not seethe inwardly and mutter outwardly, looking down on a thousand ages, spitting clouds and wind — so that even the enterprises of Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou are not worth their glance? Yet ask them about mind and nature, and they stare and their tongues are tied. Talk with them of the wonder of mind, and they cannot help clearing their throats and beating time. Talk with them of the Buddha, and they look away and do not turn their heads. Ah — to know there is a mind and not know there is a Buddha is like knowing two and five but not knowing ten. Therefore the way and its arts are not clear, and even men of brilliance and heroism cannot escape sitting in blindness here. This is not the fault of knowing; it is truly the fault of not knowing. Nor is it the fault of not knowing; it is truly the fault of not believing the mind. Yet I would suggest it is not truly a failure of belief: it is that no one has ever told them with a true mind. If morning and evening one steeped and dyed them with true mind and true words, though they could not believe of themselves, they too would be transformed along with it. The gentlemen of the world, in what they hear and see from birth, have only the ordinary fare of ear and eye; even heaven-endowed intelligence would be transformed along with that as well. Hence it is said: custom moves men, and even the worthy do not escape it. These words are to be feared. Alas — the sigh of the long night: for whom is it raised? I have now placed myself amid the empty mountains and great marshes of the East Sea, braving danger and treading on the brink of ruin, several times barely escaping the tiger’s mouth. Those who know me say I am grieved at heart; those who do not know me ask what I am seeking. This is why I hold the sigh of the long night and weep tears that race with the East Sea. And yet: when one tube of ash flies, spring is born through the whole earth; when one leaf leaves the branch, autumn arrives through all the sky. It is only that the response is not deep enough, and so the answer does not come. In recent years two or three gentlemen of this land have possessed a great man’s bones and believed in their own minds; the sweat of delight soaks both their armpits, and a mild and harmonious tune is about to appear. I shall have my bones dissolved into the long waves — what regret is left? The scholar Wang Muchang and the scholar Zhou Shifu came in the winter of the guisi year to the sea to pay their respects. Their savor of the Way was natural, without a hair’s breadth of cramped worldly habit. I sighed deeply that they are rare men indeed. And yet — Muchang, Muchang; Shiwen, Shiwen — both know what they originally have and are willing to seek it. My hope for you two is not that you become buddhas, but that you manifest the bodies of magistrates and laymen and speak the Dharma. Then you will see the roots of prajñā deepen, and though custom is thick, by steaming and transformation the benighted crowds of this land, both men and things, will all be settled and nourished, and be born in the land of Ultimate Bliss. Strive at it, strive at it. What more shall I say?
Instructions to the Scholar Du

Confucius said: you may take away the commander of a whole army, but you cannot take away the will of even a common man. And again: he dwelt in retirement and sought his will — what, then, was he seeking? Mencius said: hold fast your will, but do not do violence to your vital breath. This is where the sages and worthies laid bare their livers and exposed their gall in teaching people. Now the mantis in anger raises its arms to fend off the chariot-rut — what, then, was its will like? I have watched the scholars of the world: one says he has set his will on fame and rank, another on wealth and honor, another on loyalty and filial piety — all of which seem admirable. Yet let him meet with a slight rebuff or insult, with anxiety or trouble, with hunger and cold, poverty and sickness, with anything that goes against his wish, and his spirit melts and his soul flags, and he moans in a misery beyond words. Let him meet with the least opposition, and he rages without heed for his life; with wine and lust he revels and forgets to live. So the will he spoke of ordinarily never proves to be the will that, as Confucius taught, cannot be taken away, or that, as Mencius taught, is held fast. There is no other reason: he dwelt in retirement but never truly sought it. Alas — rebuff and insult, anxiety and trouble, hunger and cold, poverty and sickness, and the opposition of wine and lust, are no greater than a chariot-rut, and a man is no smaller than a mantis. Yet he never once raises a single anger to fend them off. Why is this? If a student seeks deeply into this, he may be spoken with about the will.
The Dream-Wandering Collection of the Old Man Hanshan, Scroll Thirteen
To Chan Master Daguan

My roots are dull and my capacities inferior; I bend beneath the habits of the dust, and so I have gone wandering among men for no good reason, thinking it of no account. Little did I expect my staff to land here — how could I have known it was held fast by my master’s power of diligence? Yesterday I bowed beneath your seat and was favored with your Dharma-affection: whole nights through, true words and secret sayings, like a spell cast over a sick dragon, with my mind always on cloud and rain. Even the Ganges could receive such deep grace. My master has come through every hardship himself, yet I sit and receive his kindness in a single morning — how shall I ever repay it? I think the buddhas of the ten directions must surely rejoice at this meeting and utter praise. This connection is no small one. In my folly I once said that Master Wan was surely also a man of the Vulture Peak assembly; had I not been brought along to Yunju and seen his very liver and gall, I might have gone through this life scarcely knowing this man. When you commanded me to write the record of Master Wan’s stupa court, I did not at first measure myself, thinking it would be easy, and so I crudely took it on. But when I reached Leiyin and saw his true traces, my breath shrank without my knowing it. Even were I to make the void my mouth and the great earth my tongue, I still could not praise his merit — how much less with the trickle of this square inch? So I earnestly prayed for the protection of the Dharma’s power and set to it. The phrasing was especially hard. On horseback I reached Tanzhe, and my thought was already more than half done; then I saw the two scriptures copied in your own hand, so grave and wondrously fair, and when I read your vow and praise, suddenly it was complete. On the evening of the fifteenth I returned to Cishou, and the next day burned incense and bowed in prayer; only then did I take up the brush and draft it. It was just finished when a messenger arrived bringing your Dharma-voice. I recited it several times, overjoyed and utterly overcome. You have put your Dharma-body to the trouble of appearing specially in the dust — it seems your compassion is too extreme. How can I bear it? I respectfully thank you without measure. The stupa record I herewith report as commanded. Its text runs to more than twelve hundred words, but the heart’s blood I have is only this much; whatever there was, I have poured it all out. In it I wished only to dot and dye the void, and I feel it has little flame or light. I beg you to confirm it and not spare your carver’s axe, so that Master Wan be not wronged and those who read may deepen the seeds of buddhahood. Only let your compassion receive it. I bow in salutation and speak.
Appendix: Master Da’s Reply

Zhenke bows in salutation. I have received your stupa record, and at once led the assembly in burning incense and bowing in reverence. Reading it swiftly three or four times over, I find no place left in me to lodge words of praise. Had you not truly grasped the bitter points of Master Wan’s heart and bones, how could your words have come out like knives and saws, cutting open the painful feelings? Not only do they bring spring to Master Wan’s withered bones; even I may rely on them to be immortal. In thus upholding the Dharma-way, how shall I repay the master of the sea-seal? Ho! When one staff divides the living from the dead, I would never dare let this circulate as a worldly truth. I bow in salutation again.

I, the attendant of Master Hanshan, on this trip out of the mountains — everyone thought it came as an utter surprise. The lord of Nalanda, coming to Yan this time, has perfectly accomplished measureless merit. Not only did no one anticipate this, but even the lord of Nalanda did not expect that this muddle-headed Hanshan would break into the noisy thicket of right and wrong and do so many good deeds: bringing to light the hidden radiance of the ancient worthies, and untying the tangled disputes of the crowd. And a man of the Way may also entrust his own imperishability to a few inches of brush. This is unsurpassed offering; with what shame shall I dissolve it? I am afraid, I am afraid. Huaijing is sending the scripture and the completed praise along with a short preface. I respectfully obey the command and will at once show the draft to Ruqi for correction. As for the verses Chaoru is holding, I have no leisure to expound them one by one. I fear that as he goes he will meet states and conditions, and in the end be driven by things. What is to be done, what is to be done? As for the man of the Way’s whereabouts, since the host has returned to the East Sea, I shall go on to the Stone Scriptures. But we must surely meet once more before parting; there are still a few words that seem indispensable. I bow in salutation again.

Receiving your compassionate inquiry from afar, grief and joy mingle. That this sick man’s heart is known to your Dharma-eye — you have been reading my complexion and taking my pulse for ten years now. Only the secret of the spirit’s brightness has long been kept in silence; how should it now escape your seeing into my liver and gall? But as to the origin of this man of the Way’s illness: at first he was attacked by an external evil that injured his true qi, so that the fire of the heart grew too great and melted the metal of the lungs. Inside and out assaulted, above and below blocked, neither gardenia nor motherwort would serve, and when motherwort was used, it turned the bowels and bladder to obstruction, and the binding grew daily worse. A common doctor mistakenly added nutmeg, and the heat increased further, so that I nearly suffocated to death. Only by the help of licorice was it relieved; and when the nutmeg was picked out and pepper was used to open and harmonize, sweat broke out over the whole body, and this man of the Way was fortunate to be revived with ginger. Those sick with the same illness who mistakenly took wolfsbane found even good doctors helpless. Fortunately the original qi was not damaged, and so life must not be harmed; one must simply regulate it slowly. Only when the true yin-water is generated, the heart-fire gradually descends, the external evil is subdued and dispersed, and the true lord is at peace, can one hope to restore the original qi and preserve the whole of one’s nature. I am grateful for your compassionate thought in asking from afar about the origin of this illness; such is its shape. Relying only on the white-curl-light shining from afar, since the illness began — though great fires and fierce flames scorch this body — within, the five organs are cool, and there is not the slightest thought of weariness or aversion. I look upon the prison of the three realms and the fetters of the four kinds of birth as nothing but light of sky and shadow of cloud. The sea-seal samādhi I once entered has all become a moon-in-water Dharma-ground and an air-flower Buddha-work. Happily the barrier of feeling has burst asunder and the lock of consciousness has suddenly opened. In time I shall drive the king of elephants with my long whip and follow the golden-haired lion, turning my steps back to the sandalwood grove: hungry, I shall eat the purple cypress; thirsty, I shall drink from Cao Creek. The wish of my life is fulfilled here. I would not dare put you to the trouble of stepping to Vaiśālī again to bestow sweet dew. I wish only to rest at peace with the nāga and enter deep into the limitless, awaiting the threefold circumambulation. The messenger returns; I respectfully send this to comfort your compassionate concern.

The marks of the world are flowers in the sky, inverted vision in a clouded eye — no longer worth discussing. Arising, abiding, decaying, and emptying, coming and going, replacing one another: the conditioned is like this, while the Dharma-nature is deeply still — what loss or gain could it suffer? I only think that the conditions of Dharma are not yet widespread and my vow-power not yet complete; before, this was a hindrance of wisdom, and now a thunderclap has come from the void, and all the various transformations, like cloud-shadows, are swept clean. Moreover I am glad that from now on I may be a man of the Way with nothing to do. This is precisely the fire-heap and knife-mountain accomplishing a cool, illusion-like liberation. This is truly the sages’ grace, and it has not been scant toward me. All other matters of right and wrong are utterly dissolved — how are they worth mentioning? If one can accomplish the supreme power of the Way, then all Buddha-lands may be reborn in according to one’s vow — so what of a few fists of stone and a ladle of water? I know my master’s love of the same body, a love beyond bone and flesh, and your shared grief, a grief that enters the lungs and liver; and so I dare send this to comfort you. It is no idle word. My own time of release is not far off. If the illusory conditions still await me, I hope to bear my staff among the cloud-mountains and wander at ease through my late years. What joy of Dharma would that be! This too is sent by the gods and dragons, accomplishing the first and rarest of merits.

My hindering conditions are deep and heavy, and I have been favored with my master’s compassion of the one body, which has received me. The spirit and effort you have spent, the many exceedingly subtle wisdoms — these are beyond the reach of feeling, how could they be expressed in words? We spoke our farewells at a lodging on the road, and I hoisted sail and went west. On the fifth of the new year I reached Tongjiang, and braving snow I condoled at Jianzhai’s house and met Master Tai. Asking after Xiulang’s movements, I learned he had already packed and would set out at dawn for Jiujiang. I at once sent a letter to Jishui inviting him to Tongjiang, and we gathered in the boat, rejoicing as we spoke of old times, like men long familiar with the factors of bodhi over many lives. Erzhan heard of it and welcomed us to meet in the Iron Buddha Hermitage. Our exchange was most congenial. This gentleman’s capacities are sharp and keen, and with Xiulang as his vanguard, within a single word the solid walls and banners he had raised all fell of themselves, and he turned his case around at once — no longer the Master Zou of former days. I set out only after the Lantern Festival. Xiulang escorted me to Luling, where I met Wang Xinghai. This gentleman has a natural frame for the Way; I had not expected that amid the dust of the Dharma-ending age there should be such a superior root and keen wisdom — the conditions of Dharma he will accomplish in future are not shallow. So I lingered two days before parting. Xiulang at once set his boat eastward; when you see Zhiren, he can give you the whole account. On the third of the second month I crossed Yu Ridge, and on the wall of my lodging I suddenly saw a poem left by my master — as though facing the Dharma-body and looking into a precious mirror. Rejoicing and leaping with delight, I wrote a verse: You came to Cao Creek and I did not; I came to Cao Creek and you had gone. Coming and going are originally without mind — who knows where the narrow road brings us face to face? Then I ate my fill and left. On the sixth I reached Cao Creek and paid reverence to the true image of the Sixth Patriarch, then at once left the mountains and came to Wuyang, where I called on General Wang. I met him in my prisoner’s garb. This gentleman’s spirit is very high; he himself came down the steps to loose my bonds, saying: You are a man beyond things, and moreover you prayed for the court — yet you have brought this strange calamity upon yourself. What crime is there? We are all the more grieved at heart. How could we meet you by ordinary worldly manners? I firmly declined his courtesy, but could not; in the end he kept me for a long talk, and I withdrew after a vegetarian meal. He further sent men to escort me to the place of exile. The road runs fifteen hundred li, and the dead lie in sight all along it. Even three-foot children carry spears and knives, and one cannot tell the bandits from the rest. At Dianbai half the journey still remained. To the south the mountains and forests grow dense, and one loses the track within a foot; on the broad plains and high tablelands there is no smoke of any fire. All day not a grain of rice is moistened, the whole morning not a drop of water drunk. In the Lei region famine is especially severe, and has already lasted four years. Pestilence rages greatly and epidemics sweep across; poisonous vapors cloud the sky and the steaming heat blocks out the sun. With empty bellies men meet disaster, and more than half die or are wounded. The misery of it is beyond words. Moreover along the coast the rank wind, the mountain mist, and the blazing sun pierce the nose and reach the heart, so that the spirit is dizzy and the mind drunk. This truly is a land of punishment, no idle name. I said to myself: unless one were made of ice and frost to the bone, how could one dissolve this cruel poison? By the shelter of all that I could bear and tame, I reached the ground of the patient acceptance of the unborn. Even carrying a spear in the ranks is no different from a Dharma-ground. Yet the spring is dry and the grass withered, and there is no wild vetch to pick; if my sustenance is not the joy of Chan, why should I worry that I may become one of the starved men of the Western Mountain? I am ashamed that in the Way I am not the equal of the ancient worthies, yet the times I have met surpass theirs. This is the victory of karmic power; why should I give a thought to life and death? I am simply ashamed that my original vow is not repaid and the Buddha’s grace not requited. I reflect that the buddhas tame living beings by inconceivable spiritual power, and do not use only one skillful means to break or to gather them; they want feeling to wither and wisdom to be exhausted, and one must know the utmost state and exhaust the source. The hidden benefit to dull roots — the true compassion is not shallow. If the conditions of Dharma still hold, and another day heaven grants the connection, and I may talk with my master of the dream-illusion Dharma-door — would not today’s events be the living proof? Only let my master’s light of wisdom shine all around: ten thousand li to the south of heaven are not separated by a hair. I look up and pray that the power of your unconditional compassion may always receive me.

Since we parted at the river’s head, three years have passed in the blink of an eye, and not a moment has gone by that I did not send my heart up among the clouds and the Milky Way. In the winter of the dingmao year Jueyin came, and I received your letter in your own hand, together with your compassionate gifts — Dharma treasures filling the box. Every kind of merit in them truly sprinkles sweet dew on what is scorched and dry and spreads compassionate clouds over the burning house. The Praise of the Patriarch Kang opens the adamantine true eye in a skull; reading it makes every pore of my body glow with delight, and my joy is beyond knowing. Were this not the power of unconditional compassion, how could it be so? Jueyin says that you have thoughts of a long journey with your staff, and since then I do not know where you have gone. This mind chases after deluded thoughts; whenever I meet with Youwu, we never fail to speak of your wondrous voice and countenance. Youwu is a rare man. When we parted the winter before last, with one needle at the crown of the head — he said himself the pain went through to his heels — his case turned around at once. So I gave him the name Layman Juefei, and he is now quite unlike his former self. Since this gentleman left, things have again been quiet. Fortunately all conditions have been shut out, the four elements are light and at ease, and nothing harms or troubles me; I can close my door in this felt hut and settle the unfinished case. The Laṅkāvatāra has fortunately been drafted. Last summer I gathered and guided several beginners and expounded the Lotus Sutra in the training ground, to repay my master’s great vow; there are several sheets of notes on it. All of this is fragmentary dregs — by no means true power of knowledge and vision. But thinking that this remnant of life is set inside the armor of having nothing to do, I feel all the more that the sages’ grace is hard to repay, and I use this to while away the years; and relying on the buddhas’ spiritual power, I hold it up to wash away the fault of defiling the teaching. Therefore I do not begrudge its worldly circulation. Just now receiving your Dharma-intent, I could not help being overjoyed and overcome. Gazing at the adamantine stupa is like facing the Dharma-body; reading the praises of the patriarchs is like hearing Brahmā’s voice; sipping Yangxian spring tea is like being poured sweet dew. I think: in this land of miasma, by what cause should I obtain all this? Let all who see and hear rejoice and gain benefit. Dayi has come again — he too is a Cheng Ying among monks. This young man’s root of faith was originally deep, though his habitual tendencies are not shallow; now that he has fortunately pulled away from them, they are much reduced; and favored again by my master’s Dharma-power receiving him, he may be expected to advance. Jueyin’s coming has greatly shaken out his breast and given him much ground for joy. It is a pity his will exceeds his strength; yet he will not have wasted this life — he may become an adamantine seed, and when he comes forth again he will surely not fail the ground of a good teacher. When he heard that you are in Mount Kuang, he urgently wished to see you, so I sent him back first to report. Dayi should arrive by summer; when he does, I shall give you the full account.

Earlier Dayi came to receive your Dharma-voice, and my joy was measureless. Knowing that your movements and rest are well, I am much comforted in my distant thoughts. Of late, as to the Cao Creek affair, I imagine that when you hear of it you will greatly clap your hands. My first thought was to have Yi go from Yan to Jin; but when he was about to set out, I thought how for twenty years he has trudged through other lands, and now his teacher has been gone more than two years — how could I bear to let him not burn a pinch of incense and add a handful of earth? So I urgently pressed him to return to his home mountain. He went back through Chu, and could not lay his body beneath your seat. This summer this phantom body has fortunately had no grave illness, only the demon of lychees has broken out all over me in sores, and the demon of the rice-porridge monks of Cao Creek has been making ghostly mischief in vain. So I am nursing my illness in a wayside hut. Just now I wished to enter the mountains, and I am fortunate that a certain gentleman has brought forth the great mind of the Way and wishes to be a benefactor. Yet he is as clear and mild as water, with great aspiration and little strength. Could my master, with his effortless wondrous power, stretch out his right hand across a hundred and ten cities and plant this adamantine banner? I do not know when the Tathāgata Precious Virtue and Majesty in the Buddha-land above will speak the Dharma for living beings, so that I may hear from afar the sound of your clearing your throat and snapping your fingers. In the new year I three times received letters from Zhongfu, whose comforting feelings are most sincere; I am deeply grateful for the shared body of the Way and righteousness. I understand he is to take a light carriage, and expect he may reach Jimen by mid-autumn to attend beneath your seat. The Guangdong provincial graduate Feng Changli is the foremost of my disciples here; his recent letter says he has already entered your room — how fortunate! I do not know, though, how this young man’s going or staying stands. If he is at the capital, I hope you will rescue him from time to time. I know the two Dharma-protectors have greatly manifested the power of courage, and there must be a response; it is only a matter of waiting for the season and the conditions.

The affairs of this land of endurance are all manner of illusions, and they are precisely what should be viewed with the Dharma-eye. If they enter the eye of Śāriputra, one cannot avoid seeing them as pure and impure. Yesterday Yongshun brought your Dharma-voice, and I learned that your staff has journeyed to the sacred peaks; my reply has already gone straight to you. As to the causal matter of the Sandalwood Tathāgata, it was fully set out in my earlier inquiry — the Buddha’s spiritual power does not depend on another. I am sending the Laṅkāvatāra Notes for you to receive into your eye of wisdom as an offering of Dharma. I am inferior, yet I know deeply that this one great causal matter was all sent by the Tathāgata and bestowed by the sages’ grace, and that here is ground for repaying that grace. I only pray that this Dharma may spread through lands as numerous as motes of dust, and that all who see and hear may together enter the self-mind’s measure of manifestation. Then though I be cast into a ditch, this life will be a thousand times sufficient, ten thousand times sufficient — what regret could remain? I only do not know whether there is some small correspondence in it. I pray you greatly bestow the golden lancet and scrape away the film from my eyes; the good fortune would not be mine alone.

In the third month of spring I urged Jueyin to return, though he was carrying illness. At that time I still thought of Zibai contending for mastery with the Five Elders, and sent a letter of inquiry. Then suddenly the Chan man Shun brought a note in a blunt brush, and I knew that he had already trailed mud and water and gone off toward the place where for ten thousand li there is not an inch of grass. I laughed at the old fool — for what business does he keep himself so busily bustling? Yesterday someone said that on the road to Chang’an there is a man who cannot manage his affairs, who stole a clod of earth from the emperor and kneaded it into a sixteen-foot golden body, making numberless people give rise to inverted thoughts; and then he flung the sixteen-foot golden body onto the crossroads for the donkeys and horses coming and going to trample. If the old fool Zibai passes that way, what will he make of it? I once recall old Zhaozhou making a sixteen-foot golden body out of a single blade of grass, and old Leiyang making a single blade of grass out of a sixteen-foot golden body. Are these two cases the same or different? I know that on the summit of the ten-thousand-fathom peak he must give a laugh. Old Red Helmet of late has been so smoked by poisonous vapors that his ears are deaf and his eyes dim, his nose stopped and his throat tight, and I do not know when he will turn over inside the silver realm and spit out this bad habit.

Red Helmet is ten thousand li from Zibai, yet from time to time he hears the sound of the Dharma being spoken amid drums and watch-gongs, and it enters the ear like smeared poison — and instead turns the miasmic smoke and poisonous fog into sweet dew, which he feasts on day and night. That is why he ought to die and does not: he sees ever more mosquitoes and gnats along the rim of the bowl, their greedy spittle overflowing the great thousand worlds. When will the fire of the three disasters rise and burn them to embers, when will the blue wind blow them away and the light-sound heavens pour down rain to wash the ashes of the kalpa utterly clean, with nothing left? Cao Creek was once called the Precious Grove of the Western Heavens; of late it has been a demon palace and ghost pit. Laughable is old man Zibai, whose spiritual power is not great: asking only for a single night’s lodging, he could not be at peace. Now heaven has sent Red Helmet to come specially to sweep it. Within eight years he has exhausted his spiritual power, washed it all away, driven out every demon faction, and will now turn a defiled land into a Pure Land and a sea of karma into a lotus pond. Old Lu has lain buried a thousand years, and only today begins to turn over and draw breath, to revive after extinction, suddenly to see radiance blazing. But the tower gate is firmly closed, and the measureless adorned Buddha-lands cannot appear at once; one must wait for Mañjuśrī to stretch out his right hand across more than a hundred and ten cities, and by the mere merit of a finger-snap behold realm upon realm without end. And if in each of the worlds of the ten directions every Sudhana, with living beings as numerous as dust-motes in a buddha-land, came to pay reverence, each could be made to enter at once the Vairocana Dharma-realm. This is the Buddha-work at the tip of old Red Helmet’s spear and the endeavor beneath his banners. Compared with old Zibai sitting upright in the Pure Land, seated in the lotus, sending forth his broad and long tongue to speak to the emanation-body great beings of the Dharma-door of benefiting living beings — how do they compare, same or different? This Chan man has come from afar to inquire after me — no less than Qishun’s walk to Huiyang; and old Red Helmet has none of Juefan’s habit of parting from Hu Qiangzhong. From the tip of my tongue the Dharma-body of old Zi appears at every moment, and stands plainly before my eyes. I respectfully hold up a bowl of Brahman incense to make offering. Only let your compassion behold it.
To Chan Master Miaofeng

I earnestly reflect: my roots are dull and my capacities inferior, my accumulated habits thick. Riding on good conditions from former lives, I was blessed by heaven with my master, who in his true compassion stooped to rescue and pull me up, exhausting his mind and strength, using every skillful means, instructing me to my face and pulling my ear, day and evening without pause for several years. Daily I deeply beheld my master’s silently creative mind, and hated that I could not leap wholly into your mind and instantly make my eye’s movement and stillness like that of a spiritual sage. But this is a clay image and earth-fetus; in the end it is hard to transform. Still, having prayed long and entered deep, there is no lack of hidden response and unseen communion. Though my feelings are crude, yet in inward moistening and secret transformation I have never failed to rely on the empowering power of my master’s samādhi of the phantom net. Clouds gather over Clear and Cool; the moon is bright in the empty realm. Since then form divides and shadow scatters, hidden and manifest at once. Though your wondrous voice and your clearing of the throat are barred by mountains and passes, yet your true body of reality is gravely held in the water of my mind. Five years apart are still the same as one day; three thousand li of road are not separated by a thread of silk. Thus, dwelling deep on the shore of silence, I enter ever more into the realm of perfect penetration. It may be said that as the traces grow sparser the mind grows closer, that as the voice daily fades the reality daily shines. My body and spirit have never departed from a single thought of my master. And yet I know my own bodily vessel is foul and turbid; this withered frame, with its evil air rushing to heaven, cannot be hidden save in vast and empty valleys, and the dust of affliction that blocks the sky cannot be washed save in a boundless ocean. So I willingly stake my life and throw it into this poor corner of mountain and sea, and set it in a place utterly cut off — as though I were no longer in the human world. Little did I expect that, silently receiving the protection of the Dharma-protecting bodhisattvas, the treasury of penetration would be opened and a single light would suddenly shine eastward, greatly shattering the darkness — a merit rare in ten thousand ages. Tracing where it comes from, both giver and receiver flow entirely from my master’s perfect, wondrous, pure true mind. Last winter when I received the Dharma-instruction, I read through a dozen or more missives and deeply saw my master’s mind; without knowing it my tears and mucus ran together. It is just as said: joy turns me over and over, and weeping chokes me, tears soaking my lapel. But what I grieve over does not belong to feeling; it lies in what goes beyond ordinary feeling — raising my eyes, how few there are. I cannot but grieve and ache. Alas, this life of mine is finished; surely it will wither like grass and trees, there is no doubt. As for the wish to requite you by serving at your side, I hold it but cannot yet fulfill it. I only pray that my master’s true compassion will not cast me off, but with mind-to-mind perfect illumination will receive me, so that this foolish one does not enter the mad road of inversion, but with steady steps returns to the road of perfect enlightenment. For the time being I am fortunate to lodge on this one branch, which may be called secluded and fine. If the waves of the sea of consciousness grow clear, I think my master’s moon of mind can bear to keep its light and not let its shadow fall here?

All my life I have constantly examined myself. In this long night I have been fortunate to meet my master — one may say, to meet kin and friends again. Therefore, since our connection thirty years ago, I have known there is a matter that goes beyond; and for twenty years I have constantly and diligently removed dung. This single thought of bitter urgency has never left my brow and lashes. Yet I regret that accumulated habits are deep and thick, and I cannot at once purify the flowing consciousness of present karma. I have failed the Dharma-grace of master and friends, and I am deeply ashamed. Since we parted, fifteen years have suddenly passed. I have truly slept on brushwood and tasted gall, painfully spurring myself on, never daring to slacken in the least. But because the film of illusion is not yet dissolved, I am still sunk in the phantom net; my mind knows it is bound, but my strength is not free. Truly it is that the sword of wisdom is not sharp and cannot cut through at once. This place where I know the pain — would I deceive my master? Then, favored to take the Dharma as my condition, I knew I must repay the Buddha’s grace, and so I made the phantom net itself my Buddha-work. The mind that bears the burden truly holds up nine cauldrons, while the disease of Dharma-attachment has added a further seven layers. I thought I was not failing what I was born with, and dared to follow the ancient worthies; this was truly mad and foolish, not what I would call wisdom. Yet fortunately I also know in my mind that it is not right, like crossing a river in a dream. I recall the abundant grace of the sage sovereign, who bestowed on me the adamantine flame that burned through the heavy darkness and made the roots of feeling from kalpas past snap at a single stroke. Looking back on former wanderings, they are all the stuff of dreams. Therefore I take this as the great joy of my life, and I know in my mind that my master will surely congratulate me. Now, though I am cast far into the miasmic sea, it is like sitting in a Dharma-ground; drinking deep of the steaming heat is like eating sweet dew. In the leisure left from carrying my spear, I face only the Laṅkāvatāra and investigate the mind-seal of the buddhas and patriarchs. Only now do I know that all my former days fell into the shadowy gate of light and shadow, and were not true power of knowledge and vision. Thus I know that the spiritual power of the buddhas tames living beings who have the conditions, and not by only one skillful means: whether adverse or favorable, all is to make them enter the gate of cool great liberation; the fire-heap and the knife-mountain are nothing but the ground of ultimate quiescent nirvāṇa. From now on, perhaps I may be said not to have failed my own inherent spirit, and also not to have failed my master and friends. Where things meet my mind, I have written them down as they came. Now I am about to finish. Though this is not the straightforward liberation, it is at least an amusement in Dharma, enough to show that the light and shade have not been idly spent. I think that when my master hears of it he must give a laugh. Dayi has come ten thousand li to be glad at receiving your Dharma-voice. I reflect that this young man has held a single word of my master’s entrustment to me for fifteen years, with a mind as constant as one day, through ten thousand hardships; yet on Chan, the Way, and the Buddha-Dharma he has never once opened his mouth. This is a true world-transcending great man, a wonder of the Dharma-gate. And now again he has come clinging ten thousand li to this place — how could I be worthy of it? Moreover his teacher and his parents are both old; why should it be only for me? So I have urged him to return, and I send this to comfort the compassionate concern of one who knows me. Yet conditions have meeting and parting, while the Dharma has no arising or ceasing. Viewed with the true eye, there is not the least trace. The sea of lands is not separated; kalpas and thought-moments are wholly gathered in. What marks of coming and going, of this and that, could there be? My master has long dwelt thus; surely you will not let a criminal at the edge of heaven trouble your still contemplation. If heaven grants me years, I shall still return with white hair to repay my first vow. Only may the joy of Chan nourish your spirit; take care of yourself in the Way.

My master takes the Dharma-realm as his mind and the practices and vows as his body; even to encompass the adorned dust-motes of the Flower Treasury he will never weary or tire. This far wilderness, though distant, does not go outside my master’s pores. Your mind of reception is like jewel-nets interwoven, light illumining light; there is no room in it for deluded thought. For years my dull root has sat in this land of miasma, and the Buddha-work I have done has likewise not gone beyond my master’s samādhi of the phantom net. But because feeling arises, wisdom is separated, and I cannot feast on the joy of my master’s Dharma-nature; yet I rely on this to dissolve the fever of affliction and make a place of coolness. Will my master think this delusion? The ancients said that wherever one is, that is one’s home mountain, and wherever conditions lead is a joyful ground. I cannot manage it wholly, but it is enough to amuse myself. The four fascicles of the Laṅkāvatāra are truly for sealing the mind. My master’s eye of wisdom is pure and clear, and must deeply illumine and thoroughly penetrate its source. Even though in this life there is no prospect of meeting face to face, life after life we shall always be companions in Dharma.

It is six years since I entered this land of miasma, and I do not know what frost and wind look like. On the sixth of the first month this year I set out southward and lodged at an inn in Xinzhou. The cold wind cut my face no less than on the frontier. Deep in the night, wrapped in my robe, I was dreaming that I stood in the midst of ten thousand fathoms of ice and snow, when suddenly someone pushed the door open to see me — it was Dayi. I was astonished and overjoyed, utterly overcome. He carried letters from old friends in the north; the first I opened was my master’s. It was as though we sat face to face in the Earth-Propping Hut on Mount Wutai, talking at night with our heads on each other’s knees. My joy may be known. Then I asked after the many kinds of merit and adornment of my master — but these are household matters, not needing praise. I once read the Śūraṅgama Sutra and came upon Ānanda’s words, hoping the Buddha would grant him samādhi; I took it for empty talk. Seen from today, not only does my body sit in the miasmic sea — even were I to enter the Iron Enclosure, my master’s foot-light would surely shine on me first. Is it an idle word that when conditions meet, they are not worn away even through exhausted kalpas? I am fifty-six this year and have not felt old age arrive; my countenance has grown worldly, but the ground of my mind opens daily. I often say to myself: if this form were not transformed, I could be content in the sea of suffering, becoming a bridge and a bed for gods and men. This narrow and inferior view my master first broadened, and now I see it more truly. Dayi’s journey to the land of miasma was truly bitter; now I send him home, where he may rest his mad mind and attend to the matter beneath his own feet. I hope my master’s fierce and spicy tongs and hammer will smelt away his habits. Thus he will not fail us, nor fail his own former mind.

By the shifting deceit of karmic power I have been cast beyond the ridges — no less than Mañjuśrī in the Iron Enclosure. My master, with the foot-light of his kindness, shines on me from time to time, no less than in the Bodhi Ground at the first attainment of perfect enlightenment. Dayi has come, and has fully received your care; my gratitude is beyond words. Only may my master’s wheel of vows daily broaden and his samādhi daily deepen. As for this paltry defiled body, to draw near and follow you as in former days — how could that ever be again? I have been in this land of karma more than three years; of meditative concentration and liberation I do not know how it stands. But what pleases me is that I have learned to be a truly ordinary man. What I have spent my days on is merely adding to the crude habits of letters and words; all are obstructions piled up over many lives, and today they all come forth. I do not know on what day I may reach the seat and make three circumambulations to seek repentance. I first set out several kinds of writing; let my master seal and confirm them for me. From afar I recall the precious stupa of Many Treasures emerging in the void; but long ago at the Vulture Peak assembly all the emanation bodies of Śākyamuni gathered, and when the tower door opened once, Many Treasures appeared. When will my master’s emanation bodies gather? Those who hear from afar cannot help their longing admiration. Even if there were flowers to scatter, I have no spiritual feet to send them by.
To Chan Master Lianchi

Formerly, when I dwelt in the Golden Realm, my master came to pay reverence at Mañjuśrī’s dwelling, and by the power of unconditional compassion received me amid ice and snow, so that I could sit and gaze upon your radiant marks, deeply comforting my long-held wish. After a night or two we parted. Since then my heart has poured toward you, and I have been diligent indeed. I left Mount Tai and was about to journey south through a hundred cities, intending to call at your seat, but karmic power again drew me to the East Sea. Truly, because I was addicted to withered stillness, I set myself in a poor corner, in the land of the mlecchas, and there vowed to establish the Three Jewels and repay the Buddha’s grace above, staking my body and exhausting my life. Gloomily ten years have passed here. Because my power of the Way was weak, I was greatly troubled by demons for fully half the days and months, so that I brought disgrace on the Dharma-gate and was rebuked by the wise. Even now I do not measure myself, but cling to my pit and fend off the chariot-rut with my arm, mind after mind unretreating — surely this is no mere former habit? I earnestly reflect that the Dharma is in its late autumn and the orthodox school is faint and thin. We rely on my master to ride the wheel of the great compassionate vow, to raise high the Dharma banner, to make both the school and the teaching flow freely, to ply calm and insight together, to hold up the Vinaya alone, and to make the Pure Land a special gate, so that mad children know where to return and the simple and honest manner may be drawn near. When Chan practitioners come from the south, I always ask after your daily life in full; I learn that your Dharma-body is light and at ease, your physical body healthy, your joyful teaching unobstructed, and your response to capacities untiring, and that your subtle regulations are no less than at Kapilavastu. How fortunate that in the decline of a decaying age we meet such a great model. Whenever I think of it, my whole body leaps with delight and every pore is fragrant. I am deeply ashamed that the bonds of karma hold me back and I have no leisure to come and gaze upon you. Now my disciple Yin Jue sends you his respects, and I humbly provide three kinds of fine incense as an offering at the time of your preaching the precepts, to pervade the four assemblies. I bow and hope your compassion will accept it.

My master sits in the ground of quiescence and extinction, and with the precepts of Buddha-nature plants adamantine seeds for the living beings of the Dharma-ending age. Such a supreme causal condition is what Vairocana wished for and what Śākyamuni praised; it is fitting that the gods, dragons, and the eight classes should revere it. As for me, with a foul and turbid substance I have soiled the Dharma-gate, and by the conditions of karmic burden I have met this stain of guilt. Truly I have earned the buddhas’ rebuke — yet I have been favored with my master’s reception. Is this not the equal great compassion that regards all sentient beings alike? Otherwise, why should your compassionate voice be so without barrier as this? In this land of miasma I bow to your letter in your own hand; it is no less than the wheel-marks of your feet lighting up the Iron Enclosure, so that those who have the conditions and slander the Dharma may be the first to receive benefit. I was long sunk in the phantom net; now I am fortunate to rely on the buddhas’ spiritual power to smelt it with the adamantine flame. Now the nature of guilt is clear, and I rely on this as a ground for repentance. In the leisure left from my running about these years, the Buddha-work I have done and the several kinds of writings rely on the mind-light of the buddhas and patriarchs as tools to shatter obstruction. With my narrow and rustic views, dwelling in a remote land, I do not know whether they truly correspond in some small part to this Dharma. I respectfully offer them to your seat and beg my master’s Dharma-eye to seal and decide for me. If I do not fall into the slander of exaggeration, perhaps they may somewhat erase former transgressions and repay what is boundless.
To Master Yuechuan of Mount Wutai

Unworthy as I am, with dull roots, I drift on the waves of the ocean of illusion; the flower falls in the cold sky. No less than a drag-tailed turtle in the mud, I have willingly fled and hidden myself. Looking back at the people of the Golden Realm, sitting upright in the one assembly of Vulture Peak, I see the white curl of light pouring eastward and the hidden depths receiving its radiance — would they not see this dhūta practicing the bodhisattva path in such a way as to save living beings? Several times I have been favored with your compassionate thought and your diligent inquiries, but because both man and state are taken away, I have not sent a single word in reply. Surely one who knows me regards all as one body and will not see heart and mouth differently. Formerly you showed me your refutation of The Immutability of Things. In my humble mind I thought you had written it casually, trying your hand at the samādhi of play, and so I did not dare add an answer; I feared it would circulate as a substantial teaching. In the blink of an eye three autumns have passed. Just now the Phantom Master came from afar and inquired of me in this poor corner; he asked after your daily life, and I learned fully of your grieving and longing, and my deep gratitude is without end. He also brought out the draft of your refutation — I had not expected it to draw blood with every stroke as it does. Foolish as I am, though no Yang Xiu with his “young wife,” I discerned its wonder at a glance. But I am ashamed that I am not equal to your mind. Because you have honored me with such deep trust, I dare not fail your expectation; let me set out a little of it. In my view, if one judges the refutation by matching names to realities, then even were Sengzhao to rise again he could not alter your words; but if one forgets the words and grasps the meaning, then even were Zhanran to appear again he would follow in your tracks. The saying goes: a team of four horses cannot overtake the tongue — truly there is savor in that. Yet when he composed his treatise with deep thought, fixing its intent and naming it, he did not say he had no view; and he took immutability as the conventional and the untrue as the true. From this we see it is the thing that is immutable, not the true that is immutable. Because things flow and change, he now reveals immutability as the wonder; if the true were already immutable, what would be the point of speaking of immutability? Hence the saying: this dharma abides in the station of dharma; the marks of the world are permanently abiding. Its purport is excellent. By your lofty view, the passages you selected from the treatise are all words about flowing and change, and your refutation of them is word for word without error, sentence for sentence with grounds; even Sengzhao in debate would bow his head and have no words. But he also explained himself: what I have composed is never different; what I have seen is never the same. I suspect you are holding him to his words and have not taken the measure of his mind — or else your view is not the same. Hence it is said: straight words seem reversed — who will believe them? If you still do not believe, then who is there who does? Moreover Sengzhao plainly points to immutability as residing in things, while you investigate it with the true. This is a difference of gate, and so the roads diverge; no wonder you go opposite ways. I hear that it was because of me that you first took Zhanran’s words — that things each have their own nature, abiding within one age — and, confusing them with the Hīnayāna claim that there is no passing from here to another region, produced this refutation. But the reason I cited them had a purpose. It is that I habitually used the meaning of the immutability of things to question the great virtuous ones of every quarter, and they all said that things change while the true does not, and everyone spoke of it as two separate halves. Yet Zhanran’s commentary itself holds two meanings; it says that the explicit text appears similar to the Hīnayāna, and so on, while its real intent is Mahāyāna: production is precisely non-production, cessation is precisely non-cessation, change is precisely non-change. Zhanran’s intent was precisely to prevent later people, seeing this passage of the treatise, from falling into the Hīnayāna view of production and cessation, of flowing and change; and so he specially held this up and brought it out, wishing everyone to know the purport of the treatise deeply and to awaken wondrously to the wonder of immutability. But the subcommentary cites only the Hīnayāna and argues one meaning, without finishing the Mahāyāna account; its concluding line, “this is discussed as immutability with reference to the conventional truth,” shows that the meanings are long and short measured against each other, though the text is somewhat obscure. My citing it in the past was precisely out of fear that you would have today’s affair. At that time we parted with a brush of the arm; in a finger-snap eight years have passed. I thought you would exhaust immutability and see through to the true mark of all dharmas; I did not expect it to be as you describe. I venture to think that this view of yours not only fails to grasp Sengzhao’s intent in setting up his thesis, but wholly fails to grasp Zhanran’s intent in setting it out; and not only fails to grasp Zhanran’s intent in setting it out, but also fails to grasp this paltry heart of mine, like a weed. This is precisely what is meant by your relation to Sengzhao: what he composed was never different, what he saw was never the same. Such is my pipe-view, and I do not dare hold it as necessarily correct. For some time I have often quieted my spirit on this, and have a place of considerable self-confidence; whenever I bring it up, it has also been out of the wish to pity a wanderer. With my foolish mind, I hope you will be easy with yourself and set this aside for now without disputing it. Only try to strive upon all dharmas and look with your eyes: is it truly changeable or truly unchangeable? If in the rivers racing onward there is truly no flowing, if in the wild horses tossing and drumming there is truly no moving, then you will see it directly, and you may not drag in the emptiness of nature. If it is truly so, then Sengzhao’s treatise is all superfluous words, and why should one stake out a snail’s horn and fight over inches? This is enough to show that I am not joining in a stubborn proof. Ha ha.
To Dharma Master Kongyin of Mount Wutai
