Ten thousand li away in this burning land, it is truly like being boiled and sold. Whenever I recall former wanderings, a thousand feet of cold ice stands jagged before my eyes, and at once I feel the coolness pierce to the bone. But when my eyes reach their limit among the clouds, the golden-haired lion does not appear, and what is familiar is hard to forget. Long ago Devadatta pushed a mountain to crush the Buddha, and his body fell into a hell of agony; asked about it, he said it was like the fourth dhyāna heaven. Only today do I know that this was no boast — it was simply his own portion. Moreover, if one in the burning house thinks of the Pure Land and is cooled, would one in the Pure Land think of the burning house and not increase his afflictions? I am ashamed of my inferiority: I once followed after the dragons and elephants of the Dharma-gate, aspiring to make some small establishment and to offer a single blade of grass to the ten directions. Little did I know that fixed karma is hard to escape, and I have sunk into it to old age. Since Master Da passed away, this mind of mine has died and is no longer in the human world. Master Miao let go his hand and returned; his light before and his cutting-off after leave no room for regret. Now, of the eye of gods and men, only my master stands alone as a banner of light. If I have years remaining and may rely on the Dharma-power to obtain one meeting and so finish this life, that would be a great fortune. If the conditions do not coincide, I shall probably not be long in the world, and it will be a final parting; then my hope rests on the three assemblies of the Dragon Flower. Zhuanyu, a son of the Buddha with aspiration, is a pity to have this illness; if he can recover, he too is the white-browed one of your seat. Recently I have had three works cut, and send them for your seal and correction. But the book on Laozi has no good explanation from antiquity; after fifteen years of bitter effort it may serve to open the ignorance of later students. As for my Doubts Resolved on the Diamond Sutra and my Sectioning of the Lotus Sutra, if they find favor with your mind, I hope you will have them circulated — that too is a gift of Dharma.
To My Elder Brother Xue Lang’en

The year before last your attendant came south with your earnest written teaching, instructing me to take the Dharma-gate as weighty. I am of dull root and inferior capacity, long addicted to withered stillness, daily sunk in my narrow rusticity. Though a single thought of birth and death glows in me and is not obscured, my habitual defilement is deep and thick, and I cannot at once concur with the unborn. Looking up to the ancients as friends, I am ashamed in my heart and have failed my first resolve. Of late I see the Dharma-gate desolate: even natural brothers like us are parted in different quarters, unable to sit knee to knee from time to time to investigate the mind and sound the reeds of this Way — how much less the ordinary run of men! Since receiving your teaching, my mind for benefiting others has gradually opened. But I often reckon with myself: in the school I lack clear awakening, in the teaching I have not studied with refinement, and the shallow learning of a late student values the ear and despises the eye, so that winning trust is not easy; the wish to transform manners and customs seems hard to stretch out at once. I often think deeply that our Buddha established the teaching with the three studies as its school; yet whenever I see later students, most of them, as you say, are hardest to establish because they do not measure the root — and if one or two have slightly keen capacities, they are possessed by mad demons, so that they slight the Dharma and belittle their teachers, and their body and mind are without the least restraint. If the root is not firm, how can one hope for flourishing branches and leaves? This is precisely what you mean by there being not one or two in a thousand worth speaking to; over this I never fail to weep. I have received your great teaching for twenty years. This spring I have for the first time forced myself to open the hall and, as usual, lecture for the assembly. At the opening of the hall, the first pinch of incense I offered to my original teacher, the great monk Shouyu. I often think that at the beginning of my shaving and dyeing I presumptuously received the Flower Ornament Dharma-seat and was undeservedly favored with my late teacher’s Dharma-affection, no less than you. Yet in what I have done to repay my late teacher, there is not one part in ten thousand. I recall that years ago, when I first went on pilgrimage and parted from you at Xue Lang, I asked where your aspiration lay, and you said: when the old master has passed his hundred years, I shall set up a stele and build a stupa for him, to repay the Dharma-milk, and that will suffice for my whole life; that is my original vow, and everything else may follow conditions without hindrance. Those words are still in my ear. I have kept them clearly in mind, and from time to time I have told them to those who know me. But I do not know whether this vow of yours has already been fulfilled. I earnestly reflect that you and I have both reached the age of knowing heaven’s decree, and all is illusion like this; even the years before death move gradually toward decline. Though the vow to benefit living beings is not yet ended, the thought of engaging with the world has turned to ash. If at this time we set aside the supreme condition, we shall not only erase our late teacher’s virtue but also diminish the light of the Dharma-gate, leaving later students with nothing to rely on and no knowing from where they come. That the source is far and the stream long is what the ancient worthies prized; that the family voice is not spread abroad is what former worthies were ashamed of. If brothers like us, whose names stand together in the cosmos, are as sparse as this, how much more others! May you exert yourself in time. I respectfully provide a stick of fine incense and some funds for stone as a beginning. If you cannot bear the conditions and fear that building a stupa will be difficult, then carving an octagonal square pillar would be even more ancient and elegant. The text need not be entrusted to another hand; I hope you will wield the brush yourself. This is my utmost hope.

I, your unworthy brother, have committed crimes without measure and brought disgrace upon the Dharma-gate, causing grief to teachers and friends; I am deeply ashamed. My first thought was to pass by my home mountain and lay my whole body down, relying on the power of compassion to receive me and perform the karma of confessing my offenses. You, my elder brother, were so good as to come out of the nāga’s abode for a time and step down to the river, and in pity to teach me, so that I feasted fully on sweet dew and suddenly felt the five organs cool, body and mind both transformed, guilt and merit both empty. This is why Sudhana’s southern journey took the great stupa-temple as its first step. After we parted, on the sixth of the first month I reached Tongjiang. Old Zou Nan welcomed me at the Iron Buddha Hermitage and first brought out the scroll of the ancestral masters’ causal conditions written in your own hand; unrolled, it was blazing with light, illumining eye and mind, its colophon running freely with killing and reviving, as though you sat there wielding your whisk. Master Zou treasures it — it is the Dharma-body forever acting as host in the hermitage. Master Zou’s root is the keenest; fortunately our former connection holds, and with a single word we struck accord, and he turned his former case around completely, vowing to welcome you, my elder brother, to spread the teaching in West River and give great guidance. Such is his confidence and his courage. If inquiries come to you, you should tame him well, so that he increases and exalts right faith and becomes a true seed of buddhahood. The conditions are not shallow. Passing through Luling I met old Wang Tang; his cultivation is very good, and his faith in the Pure Land is single and devoted — though judging by what he says, it seems not to be his true intent. On the third of the second month I crossed Yu Ridge, and on the sixth I visited Nanhua and paid reverence to the Sixth Patriarch. Seeing how utterly excellent its mountains and rivers and their configuration are, I do not wonder that seventeen hundred men flowed out from here. We followers of the Buddha cannot but pay reverence there once. On the nineteenth I reached Guangzhou and looked up Chen Yishan — he had already become a thing of the past. I then heard that old Ou Lun was still alive, and was about to hire a boat to visit his house, when word came that he had passed away three months before. Losing two close friends in a distant land is truly to be mourned. It used to be said that the south seas teemed with life and that its manners were simple and generous; now it is exceedingly cold and thin. The year’s famine is extraordinary, rice and grain soar in price, and the people have no means to live. From the seventh month of last autumn until now there has been no rain; the fields have no farmers, and every household has its bandits. Lei Yang is worst of all. From the provincial capital to the place of exile the road runs fifteen hundred li; Lei has had three years of disaster, its people and goods wasted away, and now pestilence rages greatly, more than half die or are wounded, and the roads are strewn with the dead. The misery pierces the heart. In late spring the steaming heat is like drifting fire. I said to myself at the outset: without the conditions of the Way, one does not know the cold of northern snows; and now without karmic power, how should one know the heat of the burning regions? The two extremes of the world’s ways I have now exhausted — yet without the one, the other could not be broken through. On arrival I joined the ranks at once and lodged this body in an old temple, exactly like a dhūta; I shoulder my halberd at the camp gate, plainly a common soldier. Only now do I know that the conjuror conjures forth every kind of form. As for death and life, danger and hardship, where is my mind not at peace? But I think of the close causes we share over many kalpas, and how I am now fortunate to meet you again through our unfinished former connection; yet I fear I may sink into the miasmic sea and be forever separated from the long road. If we meet by chance at a fork in the road, how could it be as now and as before? Surely my master’s light of wisdom shines all around and will receive me with the power of equal compassion, and will never abandon this karmically-illusory being because of his stains of guilt. What else is there to say? Grieving at this Dharma-ending age, mindful of repaying the Buddha’s grace, I wish you, elder brother, to strive for the Dharma, to respect and cherish yourself.

Since that one night on the riverbank, when I was favored with a sprinkling of sweet dew, I have gone straight into the land of miasma, and it has served throughout to drive off the steaming heat and dissolve the fever of affliction. How deep is the samādhi you have bestowed on me! All my life I have had thin conditions with the great Dharma: untaught in youth and unknowing in old age. Lately, in the leisure left from carrying my spear, I have strenuously investigated the Laṅkāvatāra and written it into notes, hoping thereby to atone for the fault of slandering the Dharma. Relying on my narrow and rustic views, I have neither followed old formulations nor yet submitted them for correction by the Dharma-eye; and in the end they have been committed to wood by a busybody — verily, a team of four horses cannot overtake the tongue. I respectfully send an attendant to present them for your seal and correction. I do not know whether there is in them some small correspondence. If I have skimmed one drop of the flavor of the ocean of nature, or the true emptiness has let through the light of a mustard-seed’s hole, then I shall not have failed this life, nor brought trouble on your seat. If a single word is off the mark, then commit it at once to water and fire; I would never dare use it to win empty fame, increase the seeds of karma, obscure my own wondrous brightness, and further block the eyes of later people. I grieve at this Dharma-ending age, where those with the right cause are few. I am fortunate to be born in this world with you, elder brother, and to walk the same gate. If in this Dharma you can seal and approve my mind, then I shall not presume to call myself a brother of Māyā — it is enough to form the connection of sharing a seat in the Tuṣita heaven.
To Master Wuyan of Shaolin

I bow in thought before the ancestral court in its late autumn: raising my eyes, how sparse it is. There is more than one thing that could bring tears. Fortunately you, beneath your seat, have come riding your vow, and with tripod-strength bear the burden — you are just at the moment to brandish the spear and hold back the sun. Last autumn heaven granted a good connection and we gathered in the royal city; with a single word we parted. When I returned to lie by the sea and saw the marks of the world as they are, all thoughts turned to ash, and I had no more wish to raise up the work of saving living beings. I only sit dumbly in the empty mountains with the phantom multitude, planting fields and earning my food, to while away the white days and see off my remaining years. Of late I hear by rumor that the Dharma-rain moistens all and the four assemblies gather like clouds. I think the lightning-and-thunder mechanism will shatter the heavy darkness and open the benighted. I grieve to think that the world’s ways decline together and most people have thin faith, taking no account whatever of the root; and with vessels of mind unclean, how can sweet dew be poured in, or a grave illness be cured? I only pray that you, beneath your seat, deeply ponder the words of the dying charge and broadly unfold the earliest regulations, so that students of beginner’s capacity take the wind and receive the bridle, stride forward and follow the hook. After that, to spread the true wind across the sky of nature and sweep away the clouds of delusion from the valleys of the aggregates is merely your ordinary, familiar, light carriage on a well-known road. How does the lofty and wise regard these mad and foolish words?
To Dharma Master Yu’an

The Buddha said that one who is beyond forty li and does not hear the Dharma falls into the offense of slighting the Dharma. I know that your Dharma-seat is within a foot, yet I do not come in person to hear it; I too fall into this offense. It is not my true mind — it is obstruction obstructing this connection. Yesterday you were so good as to visit me in vain; at the sight of you I was most glad, and then, moreover, grieved. You, beneath your seat, are so excessive in your austerities. Diligence, firm and unshakable, is indeed the vanguard of one who spreads the Dharma; but to abandon the root and grasp the branch is the first of follies. The body is the root of the Way; the heavy is the root of the light. Yet you, for the sake of one meal, would harm your life and torture your form for the crowd in order to win reputation — this is folly indeed. Are you not one who does not know weight and lightness? The ancients said that where a single thought is wholly true, a peck of gold a day is no excess. Is your understanding such that you are not at ease in what is wholly true? Vimalakīrti said: to one who is equal toward food, the Dharma is also equal. Do you take this as meaning that not favoring the crowd is equality? But if he does not favor the crowd, then as for those who make offerings to me, they are not named a field of merit — what does that mean? Yongjia said that the illusory empty body is precisely the Dharma-body. Now you harm the Dharma-body yourself and injure the life of wisdom — can you be called one who knows the Dharma? To speak the Dharma without knowing the Dharma, how will you be a model for gods and men and a rule for coming students? Those who intend not to favor others point to Cao Shan’s not receiving food. But judged by your case, if you would carry out Cao Shan’s words, must you be counted with Bo Yi and Shu Qi before you succeed? Laughable is your seat: speaking the Dharma without knowing the Dharma, acting for yourself and not for others, knowing the light and not the heavy, reckoning on death and not on life — these are all inverted views. These words of mine are much like adding frost to snow. I now offer you certain worldly provisions as your need for opening the fast. If you will not eat, I shall not meet you face to face again. Moreover I cannot come in person, and have specially sent Rushan to bow three times in your place and urge you to turn the wheel of Dharma.

The reason I comfort you with bitter words is that my regard for the Dharma is deep. I grieve that this Dharma-ending age is so sparse, that raising my eyes I see no kin. Fortunately we rely on you, who cherish the resolve to brandish a spear and hold back the sun; my admiration cannot be restrained. But the desolation here is not something ordinary feeling can know — it is simply that I, having so often been a traveler, particularly pity the guest. I think how you, by the power of the two gifts, bear the burden on one shoulder. Days and months are impermanent, and the strength of the body is limited. I only fear that if the spirit is insufficient, the joy of Dharma will not be full — then with what will you fill gods and men? That the body is the root of Dharma is no idle word. I know in my mind that your inner secret intent lies precisely beyond words. As for the gate of illusion, it too borrows the vigor of the body as a contributing condition. There has never been an ancient who did not borrow medicine and stone to nourish and guard the four elements, since the four elements are illusory things and are originally one’s own household goods. Reading your Dharma-words, they are stern as frost and snow, with the bearing of pine and cypress. But when the snow melts, the pine and cypress shake out their color — does this not depend on the warm spring to bring them forth? I only wish that your house be full of warm spring, so that grass and trees all become spring. It is because I have great hope that you will be a weight for the Dharma-gate that I dare be so garrulous.

Since we parted, four years have passed in a blur. Truly, ten thousand li and a single inch of heart: a thousand autumns are as one day. What I count fortunate is that my hair grows daily whiter while my heart grows daily redder, my form daily transforms while my thoughts daily dissolve. Formerly I heard that when the great fire burns, this land of mine is at peace; now I see that the old barbarian truly did not deceive me. Since entering the land of miasma, within a few days I made the Laṅkāvatāra my bed and my food. In the midst of fierce flame and poisonous fog I have these household goods, a true pearl of clear water, making this body and mind like cloth washed in fire. Whenever I sit beneath the bodhi tree, I deeply think of the old barbarian who carried this one branch of seed across the sea — and was fortunate to find the firewood-seller to tend and irrigate it, so that it spread its branches and sheltered gods and men. Now for two thousand years no one has looked after it. In the leisure left from carrying my spear, this man of guilt works at its foot: at dawn I clear the weeds, and with the moon I shoulder my hoe and return. Gradually I feel the living intent well up and flourish. The source of Cao Creek was blocked and choked, and I have opened and dredged it again. Of that there are certain words; I send them for your Dharma-eye to see, enough to show that this man of guilt in this place does not dare forget the family estate and be false to the utmost grace. Long ago on the day I was banished, old man Zibai, at Mount Kuang, made a vow before the Three Jewels to recite the Lotus Sutra a hundred times to seek protection. Now it has come back upon the man himself, and so I led my disciples to fulfill the vow in this felt hut. In the intervals of recitation I expound it for the assembly and mark out its great purport, calling it Beating Time. I send it with this for your correction, to show the livelihood of Red Helmet beneath the burning sky in a burning house. A laugh.
To Dharma Master Jiaoguang

This decayed fellow’s burden of guilt has brought disgrace upon the Dharma-gate. I know my shame and have no place to repent. What I count fortunate is that the power of the good teachers has protected me, so that I have long survived in the land of miasma. I often think of your honored seat surrounded by ten thousand fingers, shaking the sound of the tide, uttering the lion’s roar, warning all the deluded; wherever your voice and light reach, none fail to receive benefit — how much more those who have the conditions of Dharma-kinship. Recently Dayi returned home; hearing that you still dwell at Zhongtiao, he must have paid reverence to your radiant marks. I send several small printed works to lay before your eye of wisdom, a slight token of my thoughts of a friend ten thousand li away. If I am favored with release, I still hope to link arms with you beneath the moon on a lone peak, laughing at the empty sky and washing away the dust and hardship of half a lifetime.
To the Venerable Yin’an

Our Buddha likened birth and death to the sea and to a river. So I dwell on the shore of the sea and you dwell on the bank of a river. But the sea has no shore, while the river runs swiftly. I have watched the sea here for ten years; I do not know how long you have watched the river. Whenever I think that your late teacher has departed and will not return, my grief is unending. I have mourned him in my heart these three years — and I do not know whether you still remember your late teacher as I do. I wish you to remember your late teacher — not that you should imitate worldly feeling, but that you should remember birth and death as a river. Confucius said: it passes on like this, never resting day or night. By what will you cut across the stream and get over? Tell me, to comfort my anxious heart. I send by this opportunity three kinds of fine incense, wishing to perfume your root of faith. Once this incense is lit, you will sweat and it will soak your back — and that is enough to make offering to the buddhas of the ten directions. This is what Haiyin hopes of you. How will you repay me?
To the Venerable Jingxiu

I have received the gift of your ancestral master’s bamboo hat, exquisitely and incomparably fine. I wear it at every moment as though it were the sky; even when I sit in my cell, my eyes are often upon it. Do you wear your ancestral master’s thing as I do? We are three thousand years from the Buddha; even today, if we keep him in mind and fix our eyes on him, it is as though we met his golden countenance face to face. But if one’s recollection is not true and one’s reliance on the teaching is not earnest, then one is no disciple of the Buddha. Can you, for thirty years, keep your ancestral master in mind as we should keep the World-Honored One in mind? For me to see the Buddha is easy; to see you and your like is hard — either this body of mine cannot reach the human world, or your mind is unwilling to be like the sea. The seal is hard because body and mind are apart. Human life is floating and brittle, and the streaming light is swift. If you can brandish a spear and hold back the white sun, then you may be permitted not to fear dying a vain death under impermanence. Idle laughter and talk — what do they ever come to? Only reflect deeply.
To Master Songgu

If a sage does not appear in the world, the ten thousand ages are as a long night. This saying has circulated long, yet few have verified it. Formerly, when I was nursing illness in a poor valley, I saw the curl of light shining eastward, and it always issued from between my master’s brows; so that all who came seeking the light from the ten directions had somewhere to take refuge, and even those who scattered flowers in offering fulfilled the Buddha-work. Since the Dharma-gate has such auspicious marks, would not the buddhas of the ten directions all rejoice and praise together? This spring I, unworthy one, sit amid evil kalpas, and the sounds of every suffering pierce my heart. Again I hear that my master is wearied by the ford and bridge, and shakes his sleeve and departs. This is the painful place where the awl enters. I have said privately: our Buddha dwelt in Śrāvastī, yet the old woman east of the city was unwilling to see him; those of later times who possess the true command said that this old woman had the marks of a great being. Now I look at the evil world of the five turbidities and the lands of every suffering: not one clear-eyed man can be placed there — and I too say that the living beings of these lands all have the marks of great beings. Speaking of this, what does my master think? My karmic conditions are deep and heavy, and of late I have again been dragged into this noisy thicket. There is no help for it that the habit of narrowness is not forgotten and the great bodhi-mind not brought forth. Yet with my master not before my eyes, the poor children of other regions pile up at the long elder’s gate with no one to rely on, just as among many stars there is no bright moon; hence the ten directions are dark. It is not only that the buddhas and patriarchs have no light — it truly makes the ground of awakening so cold and faint. With the whole earth frozen, would it not freeze the Dharma-body to death? It makes one endlessly grieved and bitter — how could it be only a sigh of the long night? This heart of mine has nowhere to lodge, and I can only join my palms in the water-and-moon light of my master and utter one word of praise. From afar I see before Bright Moon Mountain, on the stone of light, you speaking the Dharma-door of self-realization to the host mountain’s spirits, making those who hear go deaf and those who see go blind. This is my master’s own-nature Dharma-joy; surely with this you while away the days and months and break through your solitude.
To Master Jingtang

Ten years, and we had just met once when we brushed arms and lost each other. Yet this moon of the mind, chill and faint — how could it not hang beneath the long pines before the steps? I recall how my master would lead the disciples, wandering and eating and resting among them; was that not provision for verse and song, and an ailment of meditative concentration? The master’s seamless stupa, I imagine, has shown its model. Who should write the record of his life and practice? When it is done, I hope you will send it to me. Whatever is composed after our parting, I only pray you will write it on a hundred feet of paper and let it straightway enter the light of my sea-seal, as a companion to the Phantom Man.
To the Venerable Wan’an

You are the pivot and mechanism of the Dharma-gate, bearing a very heavy burden; you ride the power of a former vow, which is truly no small matter. Since we parted at Clear and Cool, though this decayed fellow lives on absurdly in the world, he has never once forgotten his feeling for you. What I grieve over is not your person but what your person is tied to; this is no idle word. Yesterday, for the sake of a great causal matter, I entered Śrāvastī and saw you once, and my joy was beyond myself; my heart dissolved like ice breaking up. Only then did I know that the roaming of dragons and elephants cannot be measured by a footpath. What comfort can I speak? In the month or more we spent together, I observed the mist-and-cloud vapor between your brows, lively and free, with a mind that holds the dust and chaff of this turbid world as nothing; your speech and silence blazed with samādhi. This comes from the spiritual roots you planted in past lives and from the inward perfuming of prajñā; what is lacking is only an outward condition to help manifest the supreme first meaning that goes beyond. Truly this is to be mourned. What we are endowed with, in being alone spiritually aware among all things — is it only that mouth and body be comfortable and full? There is a truly great wealth, a wealth to be sought within oneself and not borrowed from others. That is what is meant by the wish-fulfilling pearl. This is why our Buddha, the World-Honored One, saw it early: he did not cling to comfort, wealth, honor, or glory, but willingly dwelt on cold cliffs and by six years of austerities won a vast enjoyment. That is why, at the single sight of the morning star, it was as though in the palm of his hand. We possess it and do not see it; therefore we willingly gallop in pursuit and, for the sake of a perilous life held in one breath, win measureless affliction. That is why, meeting with a condition of love, we cast it off like spittle and snivel. Were one to weigh their lightness and weight, it would be no less than comparing shooting a bird at a thousand fathoms with the Marquis of Sui’s pearl. How do you regard yourself? I pray you respect and preserve yourself, and by no means slight or abandon yourself, steeped and drowned in wine, so that kin and friends must grieve for you. As for this decayed fellow, he is a rotten ailanthus, useless timber; he does not dare cast a sidelong glance at the human world. Thinking how hard it is to meet you face to face, and grateful for your noble friendship and the singular weight of your regard for me, I dare repay you with words. The streaming light is hard to tie down; days and months deceive us. I only wish you to strive over every inch of time, and to respect and cherish yourself.
To My Original Teacher Old Man Mei

I, your disciple, examine the source of my guilt and find it past repentance. I received this body from my parents, grace from my ruler, instruction from my teacher, understanding from my friends, the Dharma from my good teachers, and food from my benefactors. For all this grace and virtue, to destroy this body in repayment would not suffice to requite a ten-thousandth part; to pluck out every hair and count my offenses would not reckon even a small portion. Even now, cast into the wilderness ten thousand li away, I am still within the covering and bearing of heaven and earth, and my four requisites are secure: above I rely on the sage sovereign, below on my benefactors, so that I am not driven to hunger and wandering. All of this depends on one portion of merit within the Tathāgata’s white-curl light. Though it is named a land of punishment, I share equally in its nurture; this human flowering-retribution I may yet escape — but the true cause of hell, how shall I avoid it? This is what I rot my heart over day and night. Since parting from my master, four years have passed in a blur. Though I sit in the arena of spears and halberds, not one thought has ever forgotten the original matter. Before, I could not even read a line of the Laṅkāvatāra; fortunately, by this place I have been able to investigate the mind fully. When I first reached the place of exile, I sat in the charnel grove and at once settled my mind in contemplation, writing down whatever I attained as it came. Without knowing it I finished the scroll. This summer I expounded it once for the assembly, and those who heard it found no great error in it. I trust it is not much idle talk; and though I do not presume to show my ambition by writing a book, it is at least enough to serve as material for repentance, and it shows that amid haste and adversity I do not dare forget the Buddha-work. I respectfully hold up one copy to offer before my master, in repayment of the grace of your instruction. I hope you will keep it in your room as a treasure for your heirs, and as talk for another day.
Words in Charge to a Disciple

You are going. Be easy with yourself, and do not let the small harm the great; do not reject words because of the person. These words are insistent — I give them for the sake of your faith. If you would seek faith, let it be as my faith. Strive at it. Do not yield to your temper; do not trust to your ambition. Yielding to temper brings injury; trusting to ambition brings madness. Small impatience ruins great plans. A man without far concerns will surely have near troubles. Small matters should be corrected; fine conduct should be diligent. Heaven’s decree is to be feared; the words of sages are to be honored. Settle your will and gather your spirit; do not take it for easy. Let your heart be trembling and cautious; guard your mouth as a bottle, and defend your thoughts as a city. Let learning daily accumulate and virtue daily renew. Vulgar custom is already deep; look upward and seek friends among the ancients. A gentleman guards against what has not yet happened and does not dwell in places of suspicion. Be like a bird choosing its tree, like a tiger leaning on its mountain. The world’s roads are most rugged; lift your feet with difficulty. Therefore the sage is born in sorrow and calamity and dies in heedlessness. Ask earnestly and think closely; learn broadly and keep your will firm. Meeting people, seem foolish; dwelling in the world, be as a guest. Do not trust to your tongue; do not adorn your dress. Be mild and still and silent. Let the body be like an empty boat and the mind like an empty valley. This is the faith of my faith. Strive at it.
To the Venerable Xiaochen

You sit upon the lion of Mount Tianmu. Do you still remember the matter of dropping your palms on the cliff and holding the pine as you stood in the snow? I think you have found, on the lone peak’s summit, the place where the ancients walked. If you can carry a scrap of cloud, it would be no harm to scatter it over my burning wilderness as sweet dew to cool the fever.
The Dream-Wandering Collection of the Old Man Hanshan, Scroll Fourteen
To Master Lan’an of Qixia

My master lies high among mist and clouds, burning pine needles and selling deer spring water — more than thirty years now. He looks on the dust-bound as on worms around a bowl’s rim, much less on an exile in this land of miasma. The Laṅkāvatāra Notes are the livelihood of one who goes before and behind his donkey beneath Red Helmet; I offer them to the great beings in the mountains, to vent a little of the poison in this place. When we meet in thought, I imagine a great laugh.
To Master Mijang Kai

Yesterday at dawn, having finished circumambulating the stupa, I withdrew to praise the sutra, until I came to: Wonderful it is, this treasury of the Lotus Sutra — deep, firm, and profoundly far, beyond any person’s reach. Here there is room for numberless emanation buddhas; therefore I sport in the grove, and with you clearing our throats and snapping our fingers, the sound must shake the great thousand worlds. Only the living beings here do not notice or know it. If your Dharma-conditions are finished, come and sit with me for the space of a meal. If they are not finished, then you should settle the true reality, and not give rise to weariness through fatigue. The Dharma-body does not move — where is it not joyful? I bow in salutation.
To the Chief Seat Wuxin

Long ago Devadatta harmed the Buddha, and the Buddha received him with the samādhi of loving-kindness, so that in the end it perfected the Buddha’s power of patience. When Bodhidharma first came to Shaolin, he was poisoned five times; and Great Master Hui Si was harmed seven times for spreading the Dharma. These are the visible outlines of the buddhas and patriarchs. How much more do we, born in the Dharma-ending age, whose virtue and Way fall short of theirs, live at an even greater distance from their time — what is there to wonder at? But the old man’s original mind is set on the ancestral court of Cao Creek, and all his life he has taken the Sixth Patriarch’s word, “I owe you no life,” as his samādhi of the illusory. He sees that fixed karma must be repaid, and he seeks that on the road of birth and death there be not the least hindrance. If he truly owes him a former debt, then let it be repaid; if he does not owe it, then it is like offering a courtesy to a man who does not accept it. Here the great treasury of light is such that not a mote of dust stands in it — only this is the place of true, great usefulness. Set your mind at ease, and strive to exhaust the Way.
To the Young Master Tixuan

This decayed fellow has thrown himself into the burning house and truly become a sea of poison. Had he not a liver and gall of iron and stone and a mind of ice and frost, how could he sit and while away the white days? All that he can bear: this fragile stuff of floating foam, this illusory birth and death. I do not know whether he can barely keep a breath alive, waiting for you all to stroke your beards and laugh long in the high sky and bright moon. Considering the dust-habits of many kalpas, nothing but this could smelt them. If I may rely on the buddhas’ spiritual power to be forged and perfumed here, so that the adamantine seed is freed of the body and shines, and even the subtle shadow-trace of conditions is utterly swept clean, accomplishing the supreme causal condition — then all the more I feel the sages’ grace, and what is one death to begrudge? By no means, sir, measure this decayed one by ordinary feeling and grieve for him.
To the Chan Man Wuxiang

The Buddha said: hard it is to gain a human body; hard it is to be born in a central land; hard it is to bring forth right faith; hard it is to hear the true Dharma. Now you, beneath your seat, have been born amid the dust of affliction, and yet possess this right faith; at the end of your years you have become a disciple of the Buddha and met a good teacher, and are fortunate to hear the true Dharma. This is the hardest of hard things. It is because the seeds of good roots, perfumed and brought forth over measureless kalpas, have met their condition and ripened — not by chance. From now on take the meditative phrase of nianfo as your root of life; not a single breath may be let slip. At leisure and in business, in movement and stillness, let it never be lost; and when you can recite it until it is wholly familiar even in dreams, then at the great limit, at the head of birth and death, there will be some small correspondence. What is essential is that all the worldly afflictions and habitual tendencies of former times be cut off at once. Throughout the six periods of the day, you must never let them rise sideways; and even if they rise, you must at once see through them and by no means remember them and again tie the karma of birth and death and become a seed of hell.
To the Master of Longhua

I have heard that the bodhisattva gave his body to feed a tiger and cut his flesh to feed a hawk. When the time came to give, it was truly hard to cut; so he made various gates of contemplation — beholding the body as illusion, beholding the world as empty — and only after a hundred thousand skillful means did he give. Why? Because such austerity is hard to practice. Now you, worthy master and disciples, give this flesh of your bodies, your hands and feet, to feed the greedy tigers among the bodhisattvas and to feed the hungry hawks among the good teachers. This body is limited; the eaters are without end. Yet you do so joyfully and without satiety, without needing skillful means, and without giving rise to a single thought of retreat or fall. Had you not, worthy master and disciples, sought the supreme Way by this means, then you have come into this Dharma-ending age to repay former debts. If you repay beyond the measure, the surplus is claimed back; and so in future the good teachers of every quarter will surely be the masters of Longhua today, and you, worthy master and disciples, will surely be the great good teachers. This is the true word of the buddhas, no idle saying. I alone, Haiyin, fear to tie up debts for a future life; I reckon constantly and repay here and now, wishing to make an offering of Dharma and settle the account by that. As it is said: to one who is equal toward food, the Dharma is also equal. This is my original intent. But at present the power of Dharma is not full and I am poor in Dharma-wealth; wait until I have saved for three years, and I shall certainly sit sprawling beneath the Longhua tree and utter the lion’s roar, shaking the three thousand worlds with the sound of clearing my throat. Then — like burning incense or scorching a finger — the former debts from beginningless time will all be repaid at once. Ha ha.
To the Venerable Yueqing

Production and cessation, coming and going, gathering and scattering, arising and resting — all are flowers in a diseased eye. If the film of illusion is not removed, one cannot but have inverted views. All my life this decayed fellow has set his will on the matter that goes beyond; amid bone-piercing ice and snow he has died more than once, and has won only a breast without affairs — beyond that, nothing at all. I once thought practice had no efficacy; but when I passed through this stretch of causal conditions, in the place where the pain pierced to the marrow, I pressed through the old latch and trigger. Before the platform of birth and death it was like entering Huangbo’s room; and when I was cast far away ten thousand li, drinking the miasmic smoke and bearing hunger, sitting daily in the charnel grove with only the Laṅkāvatāra to read, I suddenly saw that the buddhas and patriarchs from the first were not of such views as I had held. Only then did I know that all my former days were sunk in the shadowy gate of illusory light and shadow, and that this alone is worth more than thirty years of pilgrimage. It seems that for the ancients to leave home and settle birth and death was no idle matter, and that to be a true disciple of the Buddha is not to be an idle person; to speak of Chan, the Way, and the Buddha-Dharma is not child’s play. What I mean by entering the Buddha-Dharma through the king’s law is this: I know that the buddhas’ spiritual power tames living beings by more than one skillful means. Today one may say: I offer this body and mind to the dust-motes of lands — this is what is named repaying the Buddha’s grace. Ten thousand li away there is nothing to send as a token; I send this specially to report my joy to you. What else is there to say?
To Dharma Master Yin’an

When I was about to set out, we looked at each other in the prison. The look of grief and joy is vivid before my eyes. Since we parted, though I sit in the land of miasma and drink the poisonous fog, I again use that lofty regard of yours to dissolve the fever of affliction. In these years this man of guilt has found no small savor of Dharma here. The ancients said: though an iron wheel revolve upon one’s head, calm and wisdom are not lost. How dare this man of guilt claim such a thing? Yet in thirty years I have been through this work, and it may be dimly seen. You know me; surely you will not think it idle talk.
To Master Nayun of Mount Fang

You, beneath your seat, sit in the room of Zao and Bai, receiving the offerings of gods and men, dipping from the waves of the sea of nature, plying the oar of the compassion-flower — ten years now among the stone grottoes of Mount Fang. The Dharma-joy you enjoy surpasses the fourth dhyāna; and do you still, with your eye of wisdom, look upon a guest who has lost his direction? I have set my body at the miasmic gorge and my mind in the cold sky; hearing from afar your clear Brahman voice, I nearly fell into no-thought. Were it not that your voice shakes the dust-motes of lands, then I must be one who hears the ten directions with his ears. I have fallen into this burning wilderness, no less than the Iron Enclosure. I once heard that bodhisattvas also do great Buddha-work in such places, and that the Tathāgata’s light illumines the darkness between two mountains, making it all a Pure Land. This is no boast of the buddhas. Lately, in my felt hut, I have made certain cases; I hold up a single leaf of them as an offering to the assembly of the nine assemblies. I think the buddhas of the ten directions, seeing this rare thing, will again sigh: Wonderful! South of heaven the wild goose cannot fly, and a foot of silk cannot pass; only Mañjuśrī’s right hand can stretch here. If you do not abandon those with conditions, I pray you receive it.
To Vinaya Master Huanyi

The ancients said: when you cut the hair, it should reach the skin; when you pare the nails, they should come near the body — for nails and hair are far, while skin and body are near. I recall the autumn when this inferior one was condemned: the Dharma-gate was shaken and gods and ghosts wept in fright. You, beneath your seat, abstained from grain and drank only water and went round and about again and again, hating that you could not take my place with your own body. Had it not cut to the skin, how could you have come to this? This is what is called caring for the Dharma-gate, sharing the same body’s sorrow and joy. Therefore I take the Dharma to heart, and wish to thank you with the Dharma. One copy of the Laṅkāvatāra is enough to repay it.
To the Assembly of Yuantong Monastery on Mount Lu

The dung-sweeping dhūta of Cao Creek respectfully addresses the whole assembly of Yuantong on Mount Lu. The Dharma-way of our Great Master, the Sixth Patriarch of Cao Creek, was greatly proclaimed in Jiangxi by Nanyue and Mazu, and in the Song dynasty it flourished most on Mount Lu, where Yuantong stood first among all monasteries as the foremost place of spreading the Dharma. Master Ne’s lofty integrity and Great Master Jue’s noble spirit — five hundred years and more to this day, the water-birds and forest trees, the sound of the stream and the color of the mountains are no different from the days when those elders ascended the hall and entered the room. Moreover the halls are towering and the bells and drums answer one another, and all has been well until now. It is a pity that the sages are already far off and this Way is unheard. You people have fallen into vulgar ways; you know only the breath of gruel and rice, and do not know that there is the matter that goes beyond, handed down from the buddhas and patriarchs. Your dark karma has grown deeper, your mind-light lies buried, so that the gods and dragons grew angry and the fire god was wroth, and in a single morning all became embers, and the jade palaces and Brahman halls were left as wild thickets. Though the fivefold succession of ages brought this about, it was truly burned by the fire of your own karma, turning a Pure Land into a burning house. Can you understand this much? Fortunately the buddhas and patriarchs have their spirits, and you first obtained Zongchi as your refuge and support. He has forgotten self and other in his mind and joined differing views into one strength, so that each of you may cast away greed and delusion and together become one life. In former days, when the Dharma-way was at its height, it was no more than a thousand or ten thousand men made into a single body. Since it is so now, why fear that the monastery will not rise again or that the ancestral Way will not revive? If from this time on mind after mind does not retreat, thought after thought is single and keen, pressing straight ahead, unswerving until death, then you may turn a defiled land into a Pure Land and a burning house into a lotus pond. And since a single tile or a single rafter all come from the strength of the ten directions, what difficulty is there? The great danger is only that the minds are not equal and the vows not firm. The Elder Zongchi came to Cao Creek and fully set out the assembly’s earnest wish: they want this old man to act provisionally as your guiding teacher. Though this is what the Dharma-gate should do and is the duty within my portion, yet this old man’s former karma is not yet dissolved and the root of guilt is not yet pulled out; how dare I act rashly at my own will and again become a laughingstock for the Dharma-gate? If I am favored with the hidden aid of the buddhas and patriarchs and the vast grace of the sages, so that this old man’s skull shines at this time, then the first pinch of incense I shall offer to pray for the sage longevity of our emperor; the second pinch of incense to repay the deep grace of the buddhas and patriarchs; and the third pinch of incense I shall offer to the great good teachers of Nanyue and Mount Lu — and it will surely reach Yuantong. At that time, when you smell the incense, you will all know the season of the Old Man Hanshan’s descent and birth. Strive, all of you; do not hesitate. Take care, take care.
To the Chan Man Zongxuan

Your spiritual root was planted in former lives, and you have not lost the right cause. Shutting yourself away in retreat to cultivate in hiding and cutting off outer conditions is precisely the true practice of our kind. But I do not know whether you have received a good teacher’s instruction and obtained the right Dharma-door for cultivating the mind. Time within the retreat is surely not to be compared with idle years. Your letter says that because you read this old man’s Doubts Resolved on the Diamond Sutra, you dreamed at night that the flesh and bones of your whole body were all exchanged, but that when you sought to have your mind exchanged, it was not to be obtained. This is because you have long steeped yourself in prajñā and your spiritual mechanism has burst forth; and because in your stillness deluded thoughts silently dissolved, this state appeared to you in a dream without your knowing it. Though it is a dream and an illusion, it is precisely the place where your practice has gained strength. If you take this dream and investigate it at every moment, and where the mind is not to be obtained apply your strength and look, then as you look and look, in time the true light will of itself stand alone and be revealed. Have you not seen how the Second Patriarch served Bodhidharma and begged the master to pacify his mind? Bodhidharma said: bring me your mind and I will pacify it for you. The Patriarch said: seeking the mind, it is utterly unobtainable. Bodhidharma said: I have pacified your mind for you. And at those words the Patriarch was greatly awakened, and so received the robe and bowl that came from the west. Now you ask this old man to exchange your mind — this is precisely the case to investigate together with that one. If this old man now asks you, bring me your mind and I will exchange it for you — what will you do? Will you understand it as words spoken in a dream, or not as words spoken in a dream? Have you not seen that the Buddha said birth and death and nirvāṇa are all like last night’s dream? I rather fear you will understand the things in the dream as substantial dharmas. The Diamond Sutra takes the six similes as the mysterious gate for entering prajñā, and the dream stands first among the six. If you can use this dream matter to contemplate all dharmas by analogy, then dharma after dharma is like a dream, and in the end unattainable; and the place of the unattainable is the ultimate home to which prajñā returns. If you have not yet understood, then simply take the case of the Second Patriarch questioning Bodhidharma and investigate it at every moment, and there will surely be a time when the dream suddenly breaks.
To the Assembly of Yunqi Monastery

This old decayed one has looked up to and honored the Great Master for more than thirty years, but has been drawn away by karma and has never once visited your room; I have always regretted that my life lacked the connection. Yesterday I held a petal of incense and paid reverence before the shrine; it was as though I were in the Land of Eternally Quiescent Light, moving and speaking among the companions in Dharma. I think the Great Master must have given a glad and gentle smile. Since returning to Mount Kuang, this old one has thought from afar of the days when the Great Master was alive: his teaching was no less than at Vulture Peak, and his regulations for governing the assembly were suited to the matter at hand, taking the Vinaya in season, refined, detailed, and thorough. As for the great virtuous ones, they had long received his transforming influence, and their roots were already mellow; moreover the branches and leaves are gone, and only the real remains. Therefore the monastery is at ease, and the four requisites are full, just as when the Great Master sat on the jeweled seat, without the least diminution. So the body and mind of the assembly are calm and still, like a bright mirror or still water — how could a mote of dust or a deluded thought find room in them? Truly, as the World-Honored One said, a monk of the Dharma-ending age who can uphold the Prātimokṣa is no different from one who is close to me. From this we know that the companions of Dharma in these mountains, from today until the end of the future, may enjoy one portion of merit in the Great Master’s white-curl light and still not exhaust it — what is lacking? What is lacking is only a single mind of resting and ceasing. If everyone lays down body and mind and each seeks alone the ground of great rest, then in all the land of Great Brightness there will be no room to seek further for Buddha-Dharma and Chan. Here not a mote of dust stands; if one gives rise to a single thought of shamelessness, one not only betrays grace but betrays oneself the more. I hear that Dharma Master Huiwen is in the mountains with Dharma Master Gude, the two friends aiding the monastery and harmonizing the assembly as in the days when they attended the Great Master’s white mallet. I only hope that in the words, “Diligently contemplate the King of Dharma’s Dharma; the King of Dharma’s Dharma is thus,” you are not blind face to face — then the Great Master is daily and nightly emitting light and shaking the earth. This old decayed one is old; there is no set time for meeting again, and so my grief increases. Words cannot express my meaning.
To the Two Dharma Masters Chaosong and Yiyu

Just now someone came and told me that you have shut yourself away to recite several fascicles of the Avataṃsaka Sutra, and still have strength left to read the commentary and subcommentary. With such spirit entering the sea of Dharma-nature, the whole world must yield you a step. I think that this old one is old, resting in the empty mountains with few about me; and so I cannot keep you two brothers out of my waking and sleeping thoughts. I regret that I was born in a flourishing age yet never saw its flourishing — and that is not merely the difficulty of being born before or after a buddha. Now the wise have all gone, leaving only this decayed thing; fortunately you two brothers remain, yet you are each under a different sky, and I cannot even exchange a word and a laugh with you. I fear, moreover, that in this life there may be no day of meeting again. At this moment all my thoughts are ash; that I hold only you two brothers in mind is because what I weigh is the Dharma-gate. In these mountains rain and snow have gone on for months; wrapped in my robe on a stone bed, I am compiling the Essentials of the Avataṃsaka Sutra, and at the chapter on the Ten Grounds a verse came to me in a dream that is most fitting to tell you. Perhaps it is the buddhas’ spiritual power borrowing this old one to bring forth you two brothers’ compassionate vows. I send it separately for you to look at, to provoke a laugh; take it as dream-talk. Just now, looking through the earlier fascicle of my Comprehensive Exposition of the Śūraṅgama Sutra, in the section that breaks attachment, it seems that beginners find it hard to grasp. If there is indeed anything in it that does not go through, I hope you will clear it for me. To forget feeling for the sake of Dharma — truly one should not hold views of self and other. The scenery of Mount Kuang is the most delightful to the heart, only supportive conditions are hard. Lately, beneath the Seven Worthies Peak, I have built a thatched hut as if within a lotus flower; it may be called the most wonderful and rare of places. To think of you two sitting and talking together would be a joy of ten thousand ages. I cannot restrain what I feel; written hastily by lamplight.
To Chan Master Wunian of Huangbo

Your mind-light illumines all, and it has been long indeed. I am unworthy in the Dharma-gate; the Way does not overcome my habits. Drifting through one life, I have established nothing. As for Cao Creek being the Dharma-ground of the Sixth Patriarch, again because my obstructions are heavy I could not finish the work. Formerly I received my master’s deep concern for the ancestral Way, entrusting Master Mei to be its Dharma-protector; at that time I had already gone to Nanyue, and the conditions did not coincide, so I failed your compassionate thought. Now I have come to Cao Creek only to settle human feelings, not daring to presume on any undertaking; moreover my years are already declining and the time has passed — even if I have former vows, they must wait for another life. Yesterday I passed through Luling, and all the gentlemen there were sore at heart over the unfinished case of Qingyuan. Just now I hear that Master Mei has moved to Qiantai, and all are congratulating one another. Their thought is to borrow Mañjuśrī’s right hand stretched out from afar to stroke that summit once and make it quickly realize this great gate of liberation, this adorned Buddha-land. Yet Cao Creek and Qingyuan are true father and son of the same bone. Only you, my master, since your vow for Cao Creek was not completed, may extend it to Qingyuan. With your mind set on bearing this Way and dwelling at peace in the equal Dharma-realm, you will surely not begrudge a single snap of the fingers. What say you?
Reply to Chan Master Wuyi of Boshan

This old decayed one is ashamed: the Way does not overcome my habits, and I am of no help to the Dharma-gate. I was long shifted about by karmic power overseas for some twenty years, lodged far in foreign lands as though hearing and seeing nothing; even when your late master greatly raised the Dharma banner, I never once sent word. In the summer of the bingchen year I took refuge from the heat on Mount Kuang, and through the good offices of Wanshi I was able to learn a portion of his wondrous Way — and I only regret that I never met him. Now I hear that your late master has entered extinction. How I grieve! The Dharma-gate has lost its support, and I mourn him long. Then I learned that you, beneath your seat, have opened the teaching at Boshan, and my joy was beyond myself. You have honored me with a letter and gifts sent from afar, entrusting me with the stupa inscription for your late master. Joy and fear meet in my heart; in righteousness I dare not firmly decline. I reflect that in the two hundred years of our Ming dynasty, Chan has been sparse and the record of the transmission of the lamp has lacked its documents. How fortunate that your late master rose up to reverse the decline of a whole age — what hangs on it is no small matter. If one cannot open the true eye and the essential teaching, then later students have nothing to echo. This is why I have been repeatedly grave and careful and dared not raise it lightly. Yet I am confident that I am not unworthy to be called one who knows your late master; therefore I enter deep into his samādhi and pass lightly over his coarse traces. Moreover the form of an inscription cannot carry a burden of detail. In the inscription I have raised only his true command; as for the rest of his actual practice, a separate record may be made. I am deeply ashamed of my poor writing; it is barely enough to write a ten-thousandth part. In it I have not dared be careless with a single word, for I fear that in future it may be taken up by the record of the transmission of the lamp, and there will be those with eyes. I hope you will instruct your disciples that they must not rashly add or change anything; it would not only harm the form of the text but diminish your late master’s light. This is to be feared. I hope you will understand it in your heart. For me it is a matter of righteousness that the Dharma-gate should be praised; and I am favored with such a profusion of gifts that my shame is much increased. I respectfully have them made into adornments for the Three Jewels, that my sincerity in valuing the Dharma-milk may not be exhausted.

Though we gaze at each other from a foot away, it is as though you were at my brow and lashes; our voices reach each other without a hair’s separation. Yet you have been so good as to send diligent inquiries, and again I have received your torch of wisdom shining from afar to shatter my darkness. Facing one another with ash-cold minds, you increase my samādhi. The thickness of Dharma-affection has never exceeded this. I think of this Dharma-ending age: the school of Chan is desolate and depends precisely on being upheld. What I grieve over is that the younger generation is thin and shallow, with few who are true; most indulge their cunning cleverness, and the thieving mind is even worse. Nothing but a great forge and red furnace can smelt these vulgar habits. I hope all the more that you will not weary of the ford and bridge but add to your tongs and hammer — this is my utmost hope. As to those of whom you speak: for the sake of the Dharma-gate this old one has had offenses of the mouth; do not wonder at them. Samantabhadra praises all the buddhas with a tongue of empty space — that is his own original practice; how could it lie in reward? You should keep silent, and need never again put this on your lips.
To Chan Master Zhanran of Yunmen

The single vein that came from the west: down to more than a hundred years of our Ming, it has hung by a thread and long been near extinction, and I had seen no one with the strength to revive it. How fortunate that you, sir, have risen in the southeast, raised the great Dharma banner, and alone upheld the way of the single transmission, opening the benighted so that the younger generation of the Dharma-gate cast off their vulgar habits at once and return to it, like water rushing into a gorge. Truly this is a great matter of the age. Last year this old one wandered in Wu and Yue and was fortunate to see your dignified bearing; I rejoiced in the flourishing of the Dharma-way and could not cease praising it. This old one is ashamed to have disgraced the Dharma-gate and to be of not the least help, and now I am old. Lately I have hidden my traces on Mount Kuang to see off my remaining days, shutting my door and cutting off conditions, waiting for one breath to end. Mount Lu has long been called the famous site of West River: not only was the Lotus Society founded here, but Guizong opened its mountain in the Jin dynasty, and in the Tang there was Chan Master Chiyan who greatly unfolded the school’s spirit; down to the great elders Foyin, Zhenjing, and others, thirty-seven men, all of them mighty in the transmission of the lamp — and it has fallen into wild thickets for more than a hundred years. Recently, through the causal initiative of Master Da, it was revived; more than twenty years since, and it is still as it was. This old one can only sigh. The Dharma-protector Lord Wang and the layman Xing intend to welcome you, beneath your seat, to glorify the Dharma-ground. Hearing it, this old one rejoices and praises. You are just now at the height of your transforming work; famous mountains and famed sites, where the land is spiritual and its people outstanding — the conditions do not coincide by chance, and I think you will gladly consent. To command your staff through the great thousand worlds and hold the fruit in your palm: surely you will not take the nearness or distance of mountains and rivers to heart.
Reply to Master Siyi Shou

In my old age I have come to Mount Kuang, shut my gate, and nurse my illness; barely a breath remains. You have sent your letter from afar and shown me your two commentaries on sutra and treatise, and have honored me by asking for a preface. Weak and ill year after year, my eyes dim and flowers dance before them, my head heavy and dizzy, I dare not unroll a scroll and look long; all day I do nothing but doze. Therefore I have not been able to read them through from beginning to end, and have not got their wondrous purport; how should I dare presume to assess them? For this reason I cannot accept the command. If heaven grants me years and my weakness and illness somewhat ease, I shall still have a share in praising them.
To Master Xiuliu Yi, Keeper of the Retreat

The confusion that came upon you the other day, I think, has already settled. This matter cannot be done by carrying anything along with it. You must strike at the place where the root of life is cut off and go straight on doing it, and no longer mind how it is with that, or how it is with me. The moment a hair’s breadth of anything remains in your breast, you are played with by it. This causal condition today is one that could not be sought through a hundred thousand kalpas; had you had this connection earlier, you would not have wandered until today. Now that you are fortunate to have this great causal condition, how can you lightly let it pass? A hundred years of light and shade are but a moment. Steal these three years of work — they will pass in the blink of an eye. Grit your teeth; turn your head and there it is. Do what you can while you can. After three years, let it be however it will be. Even if you do not awaken to the Way, you will at least have fulfilled this first resolve of studying the Way — and that is the first step out of birth and death. How can you beat the retreat drum the moment you leave the gate? From now on set it down solidly and pay no more heed to how it is with that. Even amid spears, swords, and halberds you must lay down body and life — how much more on level ground in broad daylight, when you see a ghost and give rise to inverted thoughts? Never be double-minded; you must simply cut it off. Be brisk and spirited, and do not let yourself be bound round by it.

The long rain oppresses one, and I have not been able to send word; yet this mind of mine has never once set you down. I know that you dwell at ease in stillness, your body and mind at peace, and that deluded thoughts have long since dissolved of themselves. But within that dissolving of deluded thoughts there is naturally a lightness and ease, a happiness — and you must not take that lightness and ease as your enjoyment. If you take it as attainment, then from here you fall into the disease of laissez-faire, seeking only a dim, continuous, unbroken quiet and taking having-nothing-to-do as the wonder. You do not realize that this disease is the most poisonous; guard it and hold it for long, and there will be no progress at all: ignorance secretly grows, the karmic consciousness streams on, and the root of life is not cut off. In the end it is like wiping dead quicksilver with spittle — of no use whatever. Just when deluded thoughts are dissolving is the very time to apply your strength and lift up the meditative phrase, to investigate keenly and lay on the mass of doubt again. If the doubt gains strength and you lean firmly on the phrase, examining it day and night, deeper and deeper as you examine, there will in the end be a time when cold ashes pop with beans. But if you settle on having-nothing-to-do and do not raise the doubt, in the end it is not true practice. The recorded sayings of Gaofeng are just the right teacher for you; and do not understand them as mysterious and wondrous doctrines. Strive, strive.
To Master Hanyue Zang

I hear that you devote your utmost to people by means of the one road that goes beyond. In this Dharma-ending age this is the rarest of things. But the consciousness of living beings is deep and firm; if a student takes thinking for investigation and the mysterious and wondrous for the gate of awakening, I fear he cannot pass through the patriarchs’ barrier, and will find it hard to escape the pit of deluded thought. If you truly work for people, you must by no means use verse and phrase to draw out beginners. Simply make the death of the thieving mind and the extinction of knowledge and views your first concern; only then will you not fail this causal condition. As for saying, “Tathāgata Chan, patriarch Chan, thus and thus” — all that is mere table-scraps. I hear that Hanhui shares your dwelling; truly he is a beneficial friend. May you both encourage each other in this view.
